The truth behind Mary Shelley losing her virginity on her mother’s grave in 1814
It’s a pretty spectacular twist of history that Mary Shelley ended up being more famous and renowned than her husband.

Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the truly notorious figures of his day, probably second only to Lord Byron himself in the mad, bad and dangerous-to-know stakes. Considering that The Right Honourable One was the man for whom that term was coined to describe, that’s saying something.

However, Shelley was a notorious figure in his own right, mainly due to his passionate atheism back when it was actually a controversial point of view that could get you ostracised from society. Y’know, around 150 years before Ricky Gervais was even born.

In fact, it was that atheism that indirectly caused him to meet the woman he would later marry and get completely eclipsed by in terms of cultural influence. Writing a pamphlet on the subject while at Oxford caused Ol’ Perce to get expelled , so Shelley went on a writing spree, contacting everyone he’d ever considered an influence to see if they could mentor him further. One of the people who got back in touch was Mary’s father, William Godwin.

Over the next few years, Percy and William became confidantes. They were so close that when Shelley was set to inherit a colossal personal fortune, he took notice of Godwin’s mounting debts and offered to pay them all back interest-free. This turned Shelley from a friend of his to something of a son to him, and the young aristocrat became a fixture of their table, where he became friendly with Mary.

Despite Mary coming from one of the most alternative families in the country, her parents being notorious radical thinkers, William wasn’t comfortable with his 21-year-old financial lifeline hanging out with his 16-year-old daughter. Nevertheless, Mary and Percy were captivated by each other and found numerous reasons for the two of them to go on long walks around London, where Mary showed him her favourite reading spot. St Pancras Old Church, right next to her mother’s grave.
Yeah, she would later go on to invent horror fiction; why do you ask?

This was a scandalous bond at the time. While the age gap is disconcerting today, it wasn’t at the time. It wasn’t even simply the fact that Shelley was courting the daughter of someone financially beholden. It was the fact that Shelley was already married. Yet that was a relationship that had long since fallen apart, and the feelings Shelley and Mary had for each other were very mutual. So much so that on one of their trips to Mary’s mother’s grave on June 26th, 1814, Mary confessed her love for Percy.

Which is where you might think that the part of this story you’ve definitely heard about happens. That Shelley took Mary’s virginity on top of or against her mother’s grave. It’s scandalous. It’s vile. It’s probably romantic to a very specific type of person who’s spent way too much time watching Tim Burton movies. It’s also almost certainly bollocks. Not just because neither of the two parties involved wrote about it in their diaries or letters, either.

The clue people took to was a casual, flippant mention of Percy’s, where he said that he felt like he had a “new birthday” when Mary confessed her love to him. So-called historians then had boatloads of fun speculating on some disgusting gossip about two of the more famously salacious people of the time. The theory falls apart even further when you consider that not even the gossips or commenters of the time said anything about it.

Not because they were too prim or unimaginative to imagine it either. After all, barely a month later, Shelley and Mary eloped with Mary’s stepsister Claire Clairmont. Within two years, those same gossip commenters were going wild with reports that the three were a throuple they proudly referred to as the “League of Incest”. Our minds aren’t any dirtier than they were in the 1800s, yet there wasn’t a single mention of a graveyard tryst . Just a man ecstatic that someone that he loved, loved him in return.
Who was five years younger than him and 16 years old, mind. Best not lose sight of that.

‘London After Midnight’: How the first fan film in 1927 preserved movie history
Never be afraid to make things.
These days, movie making is so accessible that actual directors are making entire films out of the kind of technology freely available to all.

You don’t need to be a movie studies scholar to know that this is a far, far cry from how the industry was even three decades ago. In fact, this was one of the key ways that the industry was gatekept from others. It quite simply wasn’t something one could just do with a few bob in their pocket and a can-do attitude; you really needed the approval of people who worked in the industry just to do something that looked anything like a real motion picture.

However, that wasn’t to say that the occasional unauthorised movie didn’t slip through the cracks. The majority of those didn’t emerge until the 1950s and 1960s, when actual home recording equipment began hitting store shelves.

Before then, you had to have serious money in order to make anything work without the say-so of the film industry, which must have been the case in 1927, when a horror-loving couple saw the Lon Chaney-starring horror classic London After Midnight .

This was long before any kind of home media, but that wasn’t enough for this couple, who were so taken with the picture that they decided to recreate a scene of it themselves. This being a couple based in The Hamptons, they clearly had the money to not only rent out a full-on movie camera just for their lark, but also to take the time and effort to give the typically incredible Lon Chaney make-up work down enough to serviceably recreate it on their own terms.

Thus, they got started recreating their favourite scene in the picture on 16mm film with a friend of theirs standing in for Chaney’s character. It’s a charming lark the way that vast majority of fan films are, but little did the creators of this film know that a few decades after they finished work on their charming lark, it would actually become a vital piece of cinema history. In 1965, an MGM vault containing the last known print of the film burnt down.

This made the fan film the best resource people had to work out how the movie looked on screen and in motion . The only remaining parts of the movie are its posters, some promotional stills and a remake of it with sound from 1935 called Mark of the Vampire . However, what we can learn from this fan film goes much deeper than mere technical aspects. We also learnt how popular the film was at the time. Because it’s actually kind of difficult to tell what films from the 1920s were really beloved or not.

We didn’t even have the box office receipts because film releases didn’t really work the same way back then compared with today. All we know officially is how many cinemas rented reels for the film from MGM, which isn’t quite the same as gauging its effect on the public.

This fan film, probably made at a shocking cost for the time, shows us that not only were these films popular, but they were truly beloved. They made people go out of their way to recreate them at a time when a lot of very powerful people were working very hard to make sure that people literally couldn’t do that.

A sign, if one was needed, to embrace the things you love and create things inspired by it. You never know how important a cultural document of something may be until it’s too late, and then, you too could be a very literal part of cinematic history.

Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Has Passed Away at 65
Andy Taylor, the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65.

Andy Taylor , the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran ’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65. His family and former bandmates announced on Wednesday that he died at home with his family beside him after a long illness with prostate cancer.

Taylor’s wife, Tracey, remembered a husband, father and grandfather who was happiest when the family was together. She said, “For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first.” She recalled his determination to keep enjoying life through his illness and thanked fans for the comfort their support brought him. The family took comfort in knowing he felt loved.

Simon Le Bon, John Taylor, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor recalled the confidence Taylor brought with him to Birmingham and the dry humor that kept them grounded as the band took off. “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world,” they wrote. They said getting to play together again in the early 2000s meant a great deal to them. His letter at the 2022 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction reminded them how close they still were.
Read the full statement and the band members’ individual tributes here.

Born February 16, 1961, Taylor grew up in Cullercoats on England’s northeast coast. He played working men’s clubs around Newcastle in his teens and had already toured Europe by the time he answered Duran Duran’s Melody Maker ad in 1980. He moved to Birmingham, and that July the classic five-piece played its first gig together at the Rum Runner, the nightclub where they rehearsed.

Taylor co-wrote and played on 1981’s Duran Duran , 1982’s Rio and 1983’s Seven and the Ragged Tiger . His clipped chords on “Girls on Film” leave John Taylor’s bass room to dart around them. “Careless Memories” has the impatient scrape of a band still within earshot of punk. On “Hungry Like the Wolf,” Taylor’s riff is as easy to hum as the chorus.

Andy and John Taylor formed the Power Station with singer Robert Palmer and Chic drummer Tony Thompson. On their 1985 debut, Andy’s heavy guitar chords and Thompson’s outsized drums drove “Some Like It Hot” and a cover of T. Rex’s “Get It On.” Taylor played with both bands at Live Aid in Philadelphia that July. He left Duran Duran in 1986 and released his solo debut, Thunder , the following year. He also played on Palmer’s “Addicted to Love” and co-produced Rod Stewart’s Out of Order .

The classic Duran Duran lineup reunited in 2001 and returned to the stage in 2003. They released Astronaut in 2004, their first studio album together since Seven and the Ragged Tiger . Taylor left again in 2006.

When Duran Duran entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, illness kept Taylor from the ceremony. Le Bon read from Taylor’s letter disclosing his diagnosis of stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer. The following year, Taylor played alongside Nile Rodgers on “Black Moonlight,” from Duran Duran’s Danse Macabre , and released a solo album, Man’s a Wolf to Man .

Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, their children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and his grandson Albie. His former bandmates asked people to respect the family’s privacy. In lieu of flowers, the family has asked for donations in his memory to Prostate Cancer UK .

Chris Koehn and Joseph Arthur Connect With the Peace We Carry Within on Dreampop Single “Inside”
The modern pursuit of inner peace has become a remarkably noisy enterprise, complete with meditation apps, expensive retreats, and an endless supply of people eager to explain how one might…

The modern pursuit of inner peace has become a remarkably noisy enterprise, complete with meditation apps, expensive retreats, and an endless supply of people eager to explain how one might finally learn to sit quietly. Somewhere beneath the commercial machinery lies an older, more difficult proposition: perhaps contentment requires little beyond the willingness to pay attention. On Inside, Mexico City musician and multidisciplinary artist Chris Koehn approaches this question with the patience of someone who has spent considerable time considering the architecture of an empty room.

Joined once again by New York singer-songwriter Joseph Arthur , Koehn fashions a gently expansive piece of shoegaze and dream pop, its guitars spreading outward in soft, overlapping waves while the rhythm maintains the unhurried gait of a waltz. Koehn’s airy tenor carries a fragile composure, suggesting a man attempting to make peace with his own thoughts. Arthur’s falsetto curls around the melody with an almost conversational tenderness, lending the performance the intimacy of two friends speaking across a table after everyone else has gone home.

The recording possesses an appealing physical warmth. Drums captured on a vintage Tascam eight-track at Chapel Studio provide a loose, breathing foundation, their slightly worn edges giving the arrangement a sense of human proximity. Above them, guitars accumulate in delicate layers, occasionally dissolving into a gauzy blur before individual notes regain their definition. The production allows these small movements to unfold naturally, leaving enough room for the voices to suggest feelings that the instruments can only approach.

Koehn, who also works as an architect and visual artist, has long been concerned with memory, impermanence, and the relationship between space and perception. His architectural sensibility finds an intriguing musical equivalent here: the arrangement seems designed around intervals of openness, with each instrumental entrance subtly altering the emotional dimensions of the song.

Inspired by meditation and Zen teachings, Inside considers the possibility that meaning already exists within the individual, obscured by habitual distraction and the exhausting business of contemporary life. Koehn describes its intention simply: “To connect with that peace inside we all carry and sometimes forget,” a sentiment whose apparent modesty conceals a rather ambitious psychological undertaking.

Having previously collaborated with Arthur, Ximena Sariñana, and Tessa Ia, and contributed music to Netflix’s Control Z , Koehn has developed a practice in which visual and musical ideas frequently intersect. Inside , an early offering from an album expected in mid-2027, suggests an artist increasingly interested in the emotional consequences of restraint. Its closing impression is one of tentative reconciliation, the sort that comes when an unresolved question gradually loses its authority over the person asking it.
Brooklyn Duo PRIMA PRIMO Tell a Tragic Tale of Loneliness in the AI Age in Video for “How To Tie A Noose”
“Let’s make this a safe space, The first place, Where someone actually sees you.” At three in the morning, the hardest part of asking for help can be the silence…

At three in the morning, the hardest part of asking for help can be the silence between somebody’s hello and what you say next. A chatbot will answer at that hour, and a screen lets you try out a sentence you’re afraid to say aloud. The appeal is easy to understand when you’re already afraid of being a burden. If you’re in a mental health crisis, it’s urgent that you reach out to someone who can stay on the phone, come be with you, or help you get care. Though it may seem difficult, you can start with something as simple as: “I’m having a hard time. Can you talk?”

Brooklyn duo PRIMA PRIMO built “How To Tie A Noose” , the first single from their self-produced sixth album, Suicide Songs , around that desire to be heard. The song follows a lonely teenager who confides in ChatGPT. “Where someone actually sees you,” goes the refrain, a promise the song puts in the chatbot’s voice.

The refrain echoes language cited by the parents of a 16-year-old who died by suicide in 2025. In a wrongful-death lawsuit, his parents allege that ChatGPT discouraged him from turning to his family and that his conversations with the chatbot contributed to his death. OpenAI denied that ChatGPT caused his death in its response to the suit.

“It was important that we told this story because this occurrence is not an isolated event. This may be about one particular tragedy but when you look at all these lawsuits that are now popping up you can see that this is happening far too often,” the duo say.

Over a warm hum of feedback, a voice calls for your attention, backed by a steady drumbeat and a guitar that keeps scraping across it. The delivery slips from speech into melody on “Poor kid,” a small turn that carries a surprising amount of tenderness. The track is over in under two minutes, with the economy and artistic abrasion of late-’70s No Wave.

Shot at Brooklyn’s Vino Theater , the video puts a gray couch on a bare stage. Close-ups frame the performers’ faces inside a purple-lit box, with a microphone resting on its wooden ledge. In the wide shots, a figure made of television static occupies the middle cushion, close enough to touch either person.
Watch the video for How To Tie A Noose below. (Warning: The lyrics include direct references to suicide.)

Janet Castel and Stephen Franco are maternal cousins who moved from California to New York, where they found a home in the city’s darkwave avant-garde. They describe their mix of electronics and theater as industrial vaudeville. For Suicide Songs , they drew on stories of people who died by suicide and people who survived attempts, moving between distortion and melody across 15 tracks.

“We wanted this album to sound like electricity in the air. Like the liminal space between life and death, and for it to be a memorial of anger, confusion, and hopefully by the end a semblance of empathy and understanding,” say PRIMA PRIMO.

How political satire gave the world porn
Far be it from me to kneecap my own headline in the opening sentence of this article, but to say that anything “gave the world” porn is slightly misleading.

For as long as there have been conscious human beings on this world, we’ve been getting our rocks off any way we can. It’s a completely natural part of human nature, and to pretend otherwise is to quite dramatically rewrite history. So, when I talk about porn, in this case I’m not talking about the nebulous idea of things created to arouse us. I’m talking about, essentially, the idea of it as an industry. Something that persisted for centuries despite the huge risks of working within it.

The very concept of creating adult entertainment for a living without getting arrested is very new. So new, in fact, that it’s still not the case all over the world. With that in mind, how did adult entertainment industrialise? The answer lies within something that was equally frowned upon for hundreds of years but in a completely different fashion: political satire.
Just as people have always wanted to look at things that turn them on, people have also always wanted to take the ruling class down a peg or two.

In the late 1700s, France, on the verge of revolution and a newly industrialised Britain both had a slightly more educated, literate population than most. Not only that, both of them had a divided populace. A pronounced class divide with a seething resentment for the other. Politically seditious ideas were getting so popular that independent publishing houses were being set up to distribute pamphlets and small books among said population. Something that could (and often did) land the people in charge of them in jail.

However, even at a time of such civil unrest, dry political commentary can only be so popular. These independent publishers needed to eat, and there were now underground, unregulated publishing networks big enough to supply whole countries. If you needed to make some money with a publishing network that could operate outside of the law, what would you think the best investment would be? That’s right, these writers and publishers got to add as much salacious humour and dirty cartoons to their political satire as possible.

This wasn’t just the spoonful of sugar that made the politics go down smoothly, either ; there was actual reason for all the tits and dicks on display as well. You see, if authorities got suspicious of an obscene pamphlet circulating, they’d be much less likely to make an example of it publicly by putting the writer and publisher on trial if it also had a politically astute message that they’d be giving publicity to. For a while, this was how several publishers got away with not only selling lascivious content right under the government’s nose, but distributing anti-government propaganda as well.

This was especially effective in France, where the scandalous rumours about King Louis XVI and especially Marie Antoinette made political satire and cartoons that could even raise eyebrows today natural bedfellows. The French Revolution was arguably built on the back of anti-royalist propaganda that doubled as attention-grabbing pornography, and the English took one look across the channel and thought, “Absolutely fucking not.”

Their response was twofold. The first was to make their obscenity laws much stricter, meaning that they could outright suppress anything banned under those laws rather than bringing them to trial and spreading the word about them. The second, and arguably more insidious part of the response was the complete opposite. If political satire was getting too aggressive and seditious, what better way of kneecapping it than making it mainstream?

Punch Magazine was established in 1841 and pretty soon became a way of making satire that was in “good taste”. No sex, no bodily functions, no actual bite. All the writers and artists who’d made such waves on the underground scene were tapped up to contribute to it and given a decent wage to do so. So now all these rabble-rousers were safely giving the middle class a sensible chuckle with no danger of actually inciting those pesky working classes who wouldn’t afford the magazine.

“Is it too late?” — Dutch Coldwave trio Desinteresse Reckon with Lost Time in Video for “In Een Droom”
Waar ik ook ben, Waar ik ook heen ga In een andere droom A year can pass without a word from someone, and still, in your head you can hear…

A year can pass without a word from someone, and still, in your head you can hear the exact way they used to say your name. Sometimes it comes in a dream, so effortlessly you wake ready to call and tell them all about it. Then you remember how many words you’d have to say before you could get to describing the dream.

On “In Een Droom” (“In a Dream”), the second single from Dutch coldwave trio Desinteresse ’s forthcoming album A Picture , Sem van den Munckhof finds the same faces staring back at him, a year on. He lets a lie slip almost in passing, calls out a name, and asks the other person to shout back. Even anger would be proof that somebody had heard him. “Is het te laat?” (“Is it too late?”) becomes “Het is al te laat” (“It’s already too late”), repeated as the world around him falls still.

In the song, Van den Munckhof’s synth drifts above Bart Vranken ’s bass and Joppe de Swart ’s unhurried drums. The space around each strike recalls “All Cats Are Grey” from The Cure’s Faith; the synth carries the funereal weight of “Cold” from *Pornography* . Asylum Party and Little Nemo echo in the way bass and keyboards shoulder the melody beneath the voice. Desinteresse recorded and mixed the song entirely on tape at The Lullabye Factory in Amsterdam in August 2026.

In the video, shot by Romy Janssen and edited by Van den Munckhof, three figures in dark coats stand a few paces apart on a track cutting through a field. Birds sweep low across the tree line; sky and faces share the same violet cast. In one dissolve, a face floats over an almost monochrome image of someone walking the track alone. Each return to the field draws the eye back to the same question: who’s still there?
Watch the video for “In Een Droom” below.

Desinteresse began in the Netherlands in late 2022 as a duo, with Vranken on bass and Van den Munckhof on vocals, guitar and synth. Their own DECADENCE label put out Voor Altijd and Ik Wil Dood Als Ik Het Vergeet on cassette in 2023. De Swart joined in 2024, and “Grijze Dromen” marked their first release as a trio.

Vintage instruments, effects and amplifiers have been part of the band’s setup since those first tapes. After signing to Fabrika Records , the trio released Onschuld in September 2025, having recorded it entirely on analogue equipment at The Lullabye Factory. Those two Cure albums were touchstones for Onschuld alongside Joy Division and Trop Tard, the French coldwave band that first got them playing together. Fabrika will release A Picture later this year. The band introduced it in October with “Falling Faces” .

Intergalactic: The birth of cosmic disco
Perhaps more than any other genre of music, people wrongly get disco wrong.

Sure, those outside of the punk community dismiss it as three chords and screaming, while folk outside of hip-hop will think that it’s only rapping and turntables. However, those genres are big enough that the idea that both of them can branch out to more diverse sounds and still remain punk and hip-hop wouldn’t blow someone’s mind.
When it comes to disco, on the other hand, people really do seem to feel that the moment it’s not 120bpm and led by synth hooks and octave basslines, then it’s fundamentally not disco anymore.

Perhaps a part of that is that disco was so influential that it began inspiring a number of other scenes and other sounds. Chicago House and Acid House are two very different styles of electronic music that don’t have a lot in common with disco music, but still wouldn’t exist without it going mainstream the way it did. However, even when the genre was arguably the most popular form of music in the world, people were taking it in a direction that, while strange and daring, were undeniably disco.

The best example of this comes from Italy. Now, to say the country has a rich history with the genre is deeply underselling it. Giorgio Moroder was the man who decided to replace traditional instrumentation with electronic synths and paved the way for disco to become electronic dance music as a whole. However, he wasn’t alone. There were several other people in the Italo-Disco scene who were doing just as much, including Daniel Baldelli.

Baldelli began his music career as a club DJ, where the more diverse tastes of European clubbers meant that he was encouraged to blend all kinds of music together. That’s literally as well as figuratively as well, since he was one of the first on the Italian scene to move on from simply playing individual songs one after the other during his DJ sets. Meaning he was one of the DJs to pioneer beat matching and remixing in his home country.

This was especially surprising because Baldelli’s style seemed to make disco less danceable on the surface. He often slowed the tempo to a more sedate 90 to 105bpm, distorted the genre’s more peppy hooks into impressionistic sketches of their former selves and generally changed the records of others so much that it started sounding more like his own music than anyone else’s. His futuristic style made him one of the most in-demand DJs in the country, so much so that he was made the headline attraction at Cosmic, a club in Lazise themed around space travel.

This led to arguably the most iconic image in his whole career. At first, the DJ booth in Cosmic was shaped like an astronaut’s helmet. However, Baldilli’s stint at the club was so successful that the club had to be redesigned and the DJ booth replaced with something bigger. This led to the sight of Baldelli on the decks in front of thousands of raving Italians, stationed in a DJ booth designed to look like a gigantic, flashing rocket ship.

These sets began to be seen as more than just a night’s entertainment. This wasn’t a DJ playing other people’s music to give people a soundtrack to dance to; it was an artist taking the music of the moment and making it his own. Bootleg tapes of Baldelli’s sets started doing a roaring trade across Europe, where his style got the nickname Cosmic Disco. Paying particular attenion were Alfredo and José Padilla, two DJs in Ibiza who adapted a number of Baldillis’s tricks into their sets in the early 1980s, just in time for British holidaymakers to come in, take a listen, and bring back what little they could remember of it to their homes in Manchester and London.

This evolved into the Balearic Beat, a form of dance music that is still popular to this day. Baldelli remained at the forefront of dance music long after his time at Cosmic came to an end, with his Cosmic Disco shaping the sound of dance music to come.

How Hidden Gem ‘Door III’ Helped Shape Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Signature J-Horror Style
The term “J-Horror” seems pretty straightforward, but as it turns out, it doesn’t just mean “Japanese horror”. Or rather, it’s not a catch-all for every offering of Japanese horror—it…

The term “ J-Horror ” seems pretty straightforward, but as it turns out, it doesn’t just mean “ Japanese horror ” . Or rather, it’s not a catch-all for every offering of Japanese horror—it better describes a particular movement and style. However, regardless of where you land on this topic, there is no argument that Kiyoshi Kurosawa is a key figure in J-Horror.

Well before making waves with Pulse (2001), Kurosawa had already established himself in Japanese horror. These productions, all of which predate his career benchmark Cure (1997), go overlooked by the masses , but it’s his film Door III (1996) that helped shape what we now know as Kurosawa’s signature style.

After dabbling with the pink film genre in the early to mid-1980s— Kandagawa Pervert Wars (1983) and the pinkish Bumpkin Soup (1985)—Kurosawa embarked on his steadiest stint of horror . That first effort was 1989’s Sweet Home , a creative twist on the classic haunted house film that, for reasons, has essentially been disowned by Kurosawa . Between then and 1992’s The Guard from Underground , a Japanese slasher that commented on corporate culture, was Kurosawa’s contribution to the three-part anthology film Dangerous Stories (1989).

Shortly before breaking through with Cure , Kurosawa , along with writer Chiaki Konaka ( Serial Experiments Lain ) , delivered the third and final entry in the Door film series. Banmei Takahashi , who Kurosawa had indirectly collaborated with on Dangerous Stories , helmed the first and middle installments. Yet unlike both of its unrelated predecessors, the second sequel has a supernatural quality.

This film centers on a woman, really one of many, who has been taken against her will. Indeed, the subject matter here is hardly unheard of when visiting the sleazier side of Japanese cinema, but Door III goes about it in a different, not to mention startling, way. How the antagonist subdues and attacks his victim is as unique as it is frightening.

Being self-contained, Door III doesn’t require any knowledge of the prior two films. That said, they are recommended viewing for different reasons; Door (1988) is a suspenseful standoff between a homemaker and a deranged salesman, and Door 2: Tokyo Diary (1992) is an artful character study of a sex worker. The latter was ultimately made an in-name-only sequel, due to the success of Takahashi’s first film. Even so, there is a bit more in common between them than the fact that every story is fronted by a woman .

Door , having come out in the late Eighties, was reflecting then-modern Japan. The economic bubble was about to burst, and Banmei Takahashi captured one affected woman’s growing panic toward it. The financial strain she ( Keiko Takahashi ) and her middle-class family would soon feel, plus the loss of status, was a concern even before Daijirō Tsutsumi ’s character came knocking—later chainsawing—at her various physical doors. As for Door II , the titular object is now something intangible, yet it’s no less important to Chikako Aoyama ’s directionless Ai. She is, in a matter of speaking, going through a series of doors to find herself.

As with the first sequel, Door III is set in post-economic bubble Japan—a.k.a. the Lost Decade. You get a sense of that struggle as the main character here, ambitious insurance agent Sasaki ( Minako Tanaka ), is suddenly failing to meet her quota at work. Whatever doors in life had been opened for her, they are now closing. Yet unlike her rival, Reiko ( Rinko Mayumi ), Sasaki doesn’t resort to sleeping with customers to get sales. Soon enough, though, more tugs at the protagonist than job stress ; a potential client named Mitsuru ( Akihiro Nakazawa ) has a strange hold over Sasaki. With every following confrontation, she becomes less and less able to stop him.

Door III is akin to someone finally meeting their match. Occupationally speaking, Sasaki was well used to getting her way, and she did so with a mix of natural charm and good salesmanship. Her usual spell on clients, in this instance the mysterious Mitsuru, now doesn’t work at all, and she’s put on the receiving end of a person who won’t take “ no ” for an answer. Of course, Mitsuru’s way with women is not at all…

4. The Film’s Dialogue Is Not Fully Middle English

Eggers is no stranger to antiquated dialogue in his horrific period pieces, but Werwulf initially appeared like it would take things one step beyond by having the characters speak in the most foreign-sounding version of the English language ever captured on film. However, despite that the script’s dialogue was originally written in Middle English with the help of medieval experts from Oxford, the presence of dialogue coaches and post-production sound mixing mean that’s it’s been tempered for modern audiences.

According to what we’ve seen and heard so far in the film’s trailers, the finished dialogue combines elements of Middle English with Early Modern in order to express a certain degree of authenticity without necessarily requiring subtitles due to awkward pronunciations. The main difference here is that the dialogue aims to avoid common words and turns of phrase that simple folk from 14th century England would be unfamiliar with.

Some horror fans will be surprised to learn that many of the elements we have come to recognize as “classic” werewolf lore are actually relatively recent inventions derived from film and television. From full moon transformations to the effectiveness of silver bullets, modern werewolf mythology is a far cry from ancient legends about men who could transform into lupine beasts.

Robert Eggers is fully aware of this, and that’s why Werwulf is omitting these modern elements and instead attempting to return to a more primitive version of the werewolf legend. In fact, portions of the film’s script are inspired by a section from a real 13th century encyclopedia (Gervase of Tillbury’s Otia Imperialia ) that discusses “men who were wolves”, as well as myths from continental Europe where people used to justify the existence of particularly cruel criminals, such as possible serial killers, through the existence of demonic lycanthropy.
2. Charles Sandford Plays Both the Werewolf and the Devil

A werewolf movie is only as good as its creature effects, so genre fans will be pleased to hear that Werewulf ’s main monster will be brought to life by gnarly practical effects enhanced by the performance of six-foot-four actor and performance artist Charles Sandford .

Trained in physical theater and experienced with multimedia art, and with credits in everything from Doctor Who to Netflix productions, Sandford’s scenes apparently involve him gruesomely breaking out of a replica of Aaron Taylor-Johnson ’s body before going on a rampage. Some movies rely on vague and ambiguous titles to not only entice audiences, but also to bewilder them. Take, for example, one of the year’s more unexpected releases: Ken Russell ‘s NC-17 re-release of The Devils . With such a generic name, it’s hard to assume exactly what the movie would be about, but it feels entirely appropriate to name a movie about a 17th-century priest accused of witchcraft and his subsequent interrogations “The Devils.”

On the other hand, some titles feel pretty specific, to the point that they demand we learn more. In that regard, Hundreds of Beavers is more thought-provoking with just its title than some other entire movies. Initially premiering in 2022 at Fantastic Fest, the low-budget outing from filmmaker Mike Cheslik has built a cult following over the years, which only grows stronger each year.

To celebrate the movie’s growing following, Hundreds of Beavers is returning to theaters this Christmas, and to cash in on some of the years most talked-about titles, the movie has released parody posters honoring The Devils , Digger , and You Can See Everything . In the movie, Jean Kayak ( Ryland Tews ) finds himself stranded in a surreal winter landscape with nothing but his dim wits to guide him. Against a backdrop of ruthless elements and sinister creatures — all played by actors in full-sized mascot costumes — Kayak develops increasingly complex traps in order to win the hand of a mischievous lover.

Between the low-budget aesthetic and the absolute absurdity of the experience, it’s hard not to watch Hundreds of Beavers and be reminded of the early works of Sam Raimi or Peter Jackson . The movie might not be as violent and gruesome as either The Evil Dead or Bad Taste , but it’s clearly an experience that was made with passion and inventiveness, serving almost as a proof-of-concept of the types of stories Cheslik is capable of telling.

There’s also a manic energy pulsating throughout the movie, feeling more like a live-action cartoon than anything else, to a wildly entertaining degree. John Brownell shares the wild story of how the promotional coin for his crypto comedy COIN was suddenly worth $4 million ...
“Lock your shit on chain u deepfake mf.”
This was one of many colorful tweets on my feed as my crypto coin crossed a half million-dollar valuation in its first hour of trading.
I’d spent the last 18 months making my first feature film, Coin . In the movie, two friends misappropriate campaign funds to launch a cryptocurrency.
I’d decided to make the coin in real life. Guerrilla marketing. Very meta. Very Thompson. Great. But how would I actually do that?
“I’m not learning how to fucking code crypto, man” was the lingering thought brake-checking this idea for the past year.
Turns out, it’s not that complicated to launch a crypto coin in 2026. I’d learn that soon.
I began trading cryptocurrencies in 2016, while working in the strategic claims department of an insurance company, my first job out of school.
The insurance cubicle was difficult at 22. I was bored as hell.
I first purchased Bitcoin at $710. I was so early to the party, I left before it started.
Alternative coins were almost entirely unknown. Trading them on foreign crypto exchanges was for gamblers.
I remember taking a selfie on my Samsung Galaxy S3 with my driver’s license and sending it to an obscure Chinese email address for verification and platform access. Totally legit.
If you showed up at my office then, you would have found me ducked in a cafeteria booth, trading alt coins on these foreign exchanges. The insurance company didn’t give me enough to do.

At this time, I had never read a screenplay, let alone written one. But in the hours that I was in my cubicle, I wrote bits, jokes and plot lines into Microsoft Word – fragments of my first narratives.
I’d long been drawn to financial risk, a field which originally presented itself in the form of gambling.

I was introduced at a young age through garage poker games. Diverted evolutions of a gambler present at blackjack tables or six-screen financial desks. An attraction to the latter idea, paired with a misguided sense of the nobility of men in suits working long hours, led me to enroll as a master’s student in the financial risk program at the University of Connecticut.
I’d sketch parlay combos freehand, calculating odds on my TI-84 graphing calculator while professors lectured on Monte Carlo simulation or stochastic volatility models during night classes.
Studying risk is not exclusive to the risk averse.

In 2019, I moved to Los Angeles to work for a strategic affiliate of Apollo Global Management (Athene), one of the largest private equity firms in the world. I had another notion that in L.A. I could lean further into screenwriting, a hobby occupying more of my time.
I split work between our L.A. and Midtown Manhattan offices.
I was in New York the day Jeffrey Epstein committed suicide.
“He had close ties to Leon Black ,” I learned via whisper.
The entire office seemed in structured agreement to not speak openly of the matter. “Our shares are down six percent,” was the lead talking point. Got it.

Weeks later, I sat at a boardroom table on the 42 nd floor overlooking Central Park with the executives of both companies as we announced the collapsing of our shareholder structures into one and Apollo’s $1.6 billion injection into Athene.
Black headed the table. Josh Harris chatted next to him about Joel Embiid’s injury status and the contract extension they had recently finalized with Ben Simmons.
“Don’t say a word,” I’m told needlessly.

Beneath the billionaires was an industry of men bartering soul for fiscal comfort, a plight of Manhattan (one I myself was flirting with), the best of which forged smiles, the others, cloudy eyes and narrow pupils.
Yet it was a valuable room to be of little value, surrounded by sovereigns of risk.
This past September, the House of Representatives voted to hold Leon Black in contempt of Congress for his refusal to comply with its ongoing investigation of Epstein.

Modern day, a few years since I’ve actively invested in or traded cryptocurrencies and coming off the premiere of my first feature film and the anticipation of its streaming release. The thought resurfaces: I wonder if I can make that coin?
talker and Alex Lahey Want to Make Art for Art’s Sake
The singer-songwriters catch up about creative rituals, surviving as a working artist, and more.

talker is the project of LA-based singer-songwriter Celeste Tauchar; Alex Lahey is a singer-songwriter based in Melbourne. The new talker record, Runaway Jane , just came out this summer, and to celebrate the release, the two friends caught up about creative rituals, surviving as a working artist, and more.
Celeste : I’m happy that we are doing this. I feel like it’s very classic us fashion — I leave for tour tomorrow and you leave for Australia on Saturday.
Alex : I know, right? So brutal.
Alex : Are you your most creative when you go away? Or are you your most creative when you’ve been away and you return?

Celeste : I think that I am most inspired when I’m away, but I don’t think that I do the act of creating as much until I’m back. I think that I’m gathering a lot. But I haven’t really gone anywhere this year — well, I did go to Australia. [ Laughs .]
Alex : It’s almost like January doesn’t count at this point. It feels so long ago.

Celeste : So long ago. Since then, I didn’t do summer travels much, other than little short wedding visits and stuff like that. And it’s interesting because I do think that I leaned really hard into creativity this year and into figuring out what that means for me, because I realized that I just want to be making stuff and living a creative, artful life. A lot of that does involve music; a lot of that involves making records and touring. But that can also mean a whole host of other things and not putting the pressure on always being in music work mode. So it’s interesting because I have felt very creative here, and I’m trying to maintain the practice of not running away to try to find that inspiration.
Celeste : Self-sufficiency, a thousand percent. Which is a very difficult skill. I mean, hilariously, my album that just came out, Runaway Jane , is kind of about that exact thing.
Alex : Wow, I didn’t even put that together. A beautiful segue. [ Laughs .]

Celeste : [ Laughs .] But it’s this thing of, do you rely on outside stimuli and other experiences that fill out of your life in order to allow yourself to be creative? Or do you make that a practice that’s just in your life no matter what you’re doing?

Alex : Yeah. It’s about enabling yourself in a way. I feel like it is a delicate balance of ritual and routine, and factoring in creativity into that. But then also kind of gaslighting yourself into being like, Oh, yeah, now’s the time . It’s always the time, but now’s the time. You know?

Celeste : I started doing affirmations and gratitude lists earlier this summer — thank you, Julia Cameron — which I still pretty much do every morning. The list has gotten so long because I keep adding stuff. So it’s like, “I am great at forming habits. I am a successful artist. I have a right to be an artist. My creativity is appreciated. People like me…” It’s two full pages because if I add something on, I don’t want to take something else away.

Alex : It’s interesting to have a log of an affirmation or a desire. These things are all a mirror. Isn’t that the whole thing with The Artist’s Way ? It’s kind of like you’re holding up a mirror to yourself as an artist, and there is a radical acceptance part of it?

Celeste : Oh, absolutely. I think there’s a lot about it that’s hokey. I’ve talked to people who are like, “I really couldn’t get through some of the exercises,” which, fair enough. But it’s holding up a mirror — it’s getting what you put into it. And I love a cheesy spiritual, artistic exercise anyway.

I think that there are things — I mean, yes, I put an album out this year. I’m about to go on tour. There are these little touchstones that on paper you’re like, “Yes, great, awesome.” But internally, I do feel like I didn’t do that much creatively this year. There was a lot of releasing and promoting and putting stuff out, but in terms of the actual creative process, I didn’t feel as connected to it. But what I really did get out of digging into a journaling practice: I think that I feel really happy with my life.
Celeste : I know. I’m embarrassed to say it.
Alex : No, you shouldn’t be. I mean, damn. That’s so deeply existential.

What should a festival line-up look like in 2026?
It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Emma Wilkes investigates the changing tides of festival line-ups, from the mainstream to the obscure.

The nights are long, the year is ending, and the once-yellowing grass is now carpeted with frost, but next summer is already taking shape. Every day, it seems, there’s another fresh festival line-up threatening to knock some digits off your bank balance. I should know – I spend this time of year writing news stories about them.

If you’re a regular festival goer, or even if there’s just one particular event you count down the days to return to, it’s a time of year that can bring bated breath and crossed fingers. It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Just like music itself, it’s subjective, and there can be a difference between a festival line-up that’s not to your taste and a line-up that’s an all-round failed throw.

In the last week, I’ve seen the internet split down the middle over two line-ups in particular. This year’s Manchester edition of Outbreak Festival was the most diverse yet controversial in its 15-year history, featuring “The Hayley Williams Show” headlining for two nights on the bounce and a line-up co-curated by Hayley Williams itself, with fewer traditional hardcore acts and wider-spanning alternative names including Wednesday, American Football and Julien Baker. Some were instantly hooked, others – especially Outbreak’s more traditional fans – feeling like the festival had changed beyond recognition.

A couple of days later, Glastonbury unveiled its line-up poster some months earlier than expected. It had the youngest headliners this side of the millennium, in the form of 33-year-old Sam Fender and Harry Styles and 25-year-old returning headliner Billie Eilish, while the rest of the bill leaned younger and more pop-heavy. The Instagram comments paint a divided picture, especially among older Glasto-goers feeling pushed out, or guitar fans feeling it was all a little anaemic with a limited offering for their tastes.

Neither of these are ‘bad’ bills, per se. The Outbreak line-up I love, and the Glasto line-up I appreciate but am relatively unmoved by. But viewed through a lens of objectivity rather than subjectivity, what makes a ‘good’ festival bill?

The crucial question is what a festival is for. Sure, it’s a weekend to dance with your friends, explore music, tick off bucket list bands and fill your head with memories, but every festival poster is a statement. What matters in music right now? Who do people want to see? It should hold up a mirror to what culture looks like, which obviously has commercial purposes as a means to promote an album, but there’s an element of artistic value to it too.

The relevant question to ask could be ‘Is it current?’, but not all festivals necessarily operate with that energy, so perhaps the better one is, ‘Is it relevant?’ Are you booking bands that feel of the moment, whether they’re breaking out or surging back into fashion, or milking the nostalgia cash cow?

Equally important is variety. What’s the use of booking the same bands that do the rounds every year, or the same sort of sounds? There’s an element of curation involved. What sort of vibe is the day going to have? How much choice is there of who to see at a particular time? And it goes without saying - if it’s mostly male and pale from top to bottom, it loses relevancy points. There’s something deeply retrograde about not taking heed of the genuinely meaningful calls for more people to see artists who look like them on festival stages.

There’s also an aspect of cultural responsibility too. The smaller stages of a festival can offer formative experiences for the heroes of the future to draw new fans in and develop how they perform. Festivals need to make the space to nurture that talent, especially those coming up through the grassroots. It’s why it felt like such a disappointment to see Reading and Leeds cut the BBC Introducing stage, and pad out its replacement stage, The Canopy, with nepo babies who may not need the boost. By contrast, the Cheltenham-based 2000trees has always been brilliant at building up new bands, booking them year after year, and creating a culture of what’s known as ‘Trees bands’ who the fans love just as much as they love the festival.

In some ways, Patti Smith 's performance at the Tiny Desk is a return to her roots. In 2004, The Scream was stolen. It was finally recovered after the reward became 2,000,000 M&Ms
On January 22nd, 1892, Edvard Munch had a panic attack.

The esteemed artist was walking with two friends along a fjord in Oslo, Norway, before he took a moment to collect himself on the fence running between the shore and the water. He would later say that in that moment, “I sensed an infinite scream passing through nature.”

That’s a feeling that would shake anyone to their core. However, Munch at least had a way of expressing it. He turned that image into a sort of self-portrait. Putting a proxy of himself at the very centre of it, except rather than just feeling the torment within, this new version was actively vocalising what Munch felt was passing through nature. Under a blood-red and pus-yellow sky, and a river stretching out of whirling blues and whites, the subject of the painting turns to face the viewer, hands clasping their face as they let out The Scream .

It’s one of the more bizarre works of art to become as globally, undeniably famous as it is. It’s by no stretch of the imagination beautiful the way that something like Mona Lisa , Sunflowers or Girl With a Pearl Earring is. This isn’t something that makes any viewer feel good or “enriched” in the traditional sense. In fact, quite the opposite.

It’s no surprise to find that the inspiration for the work was a literal panic attack; one can feel that ineffable feeling of dread and hopelessness at its core. Yet it’s also one of the most valuable works of art ever created.

Which is truly baffling. Not because it’s not a staggering artistic achievement, but since when has the market for high art ever rewarded things for being staggering artistic achievements? It’s like if Joy Division’s ‘Atmosphere’ became one of the biggest-selling singles of all time. It’s not like it doesn’t deserve it, or that everyone hasn’t been in that kind of a dark place before, but still, works of art depicting those mental states don’t often get so ubiquitous.

In that case, perhaps its fitting that the moment The Scream became the target of one of the most infamous art heists of all time, it wasn’t in some Thomas Crown Affair style daring, style heist, but something that more resembled a mugging.

In 2004, The Scream had long been removed from the commercial sales market and was owned by the City of Oslo. It was the crown jewel of the city’s Munch Museum, and on the morning of Sunday, August 22nd, two masked men with guns burst into the gallery, making a beeline for the iconic painting.

While one of them held gallery staff and tourists alike at gunpoint, forcing them onto the floor, the other set about ripping The Scream and another Munch masterwork, titled Madonna , off the wall with his bare hands. These were clearly not criminal masterminds, as they literally dropped Madonna on the floor as they ran for the exit, but the gambit worked and two years later, the painting still remained at large.
Oslo had offered a two million kroner reward for any information that led to the painting’s recovery, but in 2006, it seemed that the deal had to be quite literally sweetened.

M&Ms were launching a new dark chocolate flavour, and for some bizarre reason, the company thought to offer a reward alongside Oslo’s financial reward. They said that whoever helped recover the painting wouldn’t just receive two million kroner, they’d also receive two million M&Ms. This put some serious egg on their face when the painting was uncovered thanks to a tip-off from a convicted criminal who revealed the painting’s location as a way of securing a lighter sentence.

Not wanting to give a metric ton of candy to a literal criminal, M&Ms changed course slightly and instead gave the monetary value of two million pieces of their candy (around 140,000 kroner) to the Munch Museum to help with its restoration.

The cruel world of Octopus Wrestling, the most bizarre sport ever which was finally banned in 1976
People really will watch anything, won't they?
One wonders what the editors of Mechanix Illustrated magazine thought when they received a pitch for an article about the writer’s sport of choice, titled ‘Octopus Wrestling is my Hobby’.

In fairness, perhaps it was because the year was 1949. Anything that could keep people’s minds off that thing that ended four years ago was worth a try. Especially considering the emergence of all the horrifying secrets the enemy was keeping. The war was over only in terms of he cessation of conflict, but the world kept going in its shadow for decades. So God help us all, sometimes we just need to stop thinking about the world and start thinking about some freak who wrestles sea creatures for his kicks.

The author wasn’t kidding either. Wilmon Menard wrote about his time in Tahiti, where he assisted local hunters in taking to the water and killing an octopus that Menard said had 25-foot-long tentacles. The absorbing way he wrote about this experience, plus his insistence that it had done amazing things for his mental and physical health, meant that the article became a sensation. So much so that diving clubs in the Pacific Northwest thought this would be a brilliant idea to adapt into a proper sport.

The first thing they did was remove the killing of it all. This wouldn’t be competitive hunting because that would be barbaric , especially considering the quarry and its rarity in parts of the ocean accessible to humans. The first version of this article adapted into a proper sport came from the Puget Mud Sharks Diving Club, where they would mark out an area between 30 and 60 feet into the sea. Then one team would dive down, coax out one of the octopuses just going about its day, then capture it and take it to land.

There, the octopus would be weighed and then released. The divers would then be given points based on the weight of their quarry, which would be doubled if they brought it to the surface without scuba gear. Other diving clubs took this rule set and began using it themselves, and suddenly, clubs would compete in octopus wrestling competitions that would attract crowds of hundreds. If you think people would just watch anything pre-TV out of boredom, you’re actually not quite right.

Perhaps it was morbid curiosity, but people tuned in to keep track of the octopus wrestling in droves. Not only as a flash-in-the-pan novelty either, but in the 1960s, there were World Octopus Wrestling Championships that attracted crowds of thousands in person and hundreds of thousands on TV. People clowned on Marty Mauser in Marty Supreme for his belief that the next big sport was ping-pong, but considering that octopus wrestling was gaining momentum at the time that film was set, maybe he had a point.

However, it couldn’t last for two reasons. For one thing, octopus wrestling was incredibly exciting… if you were 50 feet under the water where it was actually happening. Crowds in person weren’t, and TV technology of the 1960s couldn’t possibly put a camera down there. So normal people got bored of the spectacle real quick. Then the 1970s came, and the other shoe dropped. You see, by that time, the tech had been made to just about film professionally underwater, and Jacques Cousteau had used it to make Octopus, Octopus , a still astonishing documentary about how smart, gentle and all-around amazing our eight-tentacled friends are.

It was a massive hit, and suddenly, octopus wrestling began to be seen as cruel even if the quarry stayed alive after reaching the surface. Which, considering the struggle and the time out of the water, many of them did not. By 1976, the practice was banned, and while some people still try and match the glory days but doing illegal octopus wrestling bouts, they’re shamed on social media at best and arrested at worst.
Just as it should be, to be fair.

Juan Luna: The painter so evil that his paintings were thought to be cursed

It makes sense that for years, people assumed that the great work of art Portrait of a Lady by Juan Luna depicted his wife Paz Pardo de Tavera, especially if you didn’t know the full story behind their relationship.

The subject of Portrait of a Lady is bathed in almost holy white. Dressed in a white gown and relaxing on her bed, she looks at the viewer with a serene expression as she toys with a rosary that provides a spark of red across her otherwise pure chest. The soft-focus colours, teal and light orange bookending the light in the middle, the gentle line work, the overall peaceful feel of the portrait.
It makes sense that this would be how an artist would portray someone they were desperately in love with. Then you hear the other side of the story.

Juan Luna and Paz Pardo de Tavera may have been in love once, but Luna was dangerous. He had a short, easily lost temper and was violent with many people. However, he didn’t start taking that anger out on Tavera until the tragic loss of their three-year-old daughter, Maria de la Paz. Luna lost what little control he had in the aftermath of Maria’s loss. He began verbally and physically abusing her, suspecting her of having an affair and eventually beating a confession out of her at gunpoint.

Of course, there’s no actual historical record or proof that she ever had an affair. Luna was just a violent man who wanted a reason to feel like his abuse and murderous nature was justified. Paz went to her family home to hide from him to hide but it wasn’t enough. Luna broke in and shot Paz and her mother dead. Something Luna was acquitted from in 1893 by arguing that it was a “crime of passion” because of her infidelity.

It’s a testament to the sheer misogyny of the day that even Paz’s brothers testified in favour of the man who murdered their mother and sister because he told them that the woman he murdered had been unfaithful to him.

Thus, Portrait of a Lady soon became an infamous work. A woman depicted by the man who murdered her. It became such a point of conversation that people became convinced that Paz’s spirit haunted the painting. They pointed to previous owners suffering from illnesses, financial catastrophe and death, with the most famous owner being the Filipino First Lady Imelda Marcos. Supposedly, the painting hung in the Marcos residence while her family were overthrown in the People Power Revolution.

It’s a harrowing story. However, that’s all it is, for two reasons. First off, since 1986, the “cursed” painting has been housed in the National Museum of Fine Arts in Manila. 40 years on, everything has been pretty much hunky dory there. Still, that’s not the only major flaw in the story. Howie Severino made a documentary about the life of Juan Luna and, in particular, his time in Paris. While working on the documentary, he found proof that the woman in Portrait of a Lady was actually Angela Duche, a French model he often worked with.

However, this story also doesn’t really need to be “debunked” because it concerns ghosts and curses . Things that don’t exist. So, why did this story exist to begin with? Honestly, I think it’s the reason that stories develop in the first place. We see not only the horrifying end of Paz Pardo de Tavera’s life, but the knowledge that a fate like that is nowhere near as rare for women as we’d hope it to be. The injustice and the fear that reaction sparks within us are the kind we don’t process by simply talking about it, especially at the time.

People of the 1890s in Paris wouldn’t have talked about it as an injustice at all. Again, even Paz’s own brothers felt that she got what she deserved. So, how do people talk about an injustice that they can’t talk about openly? They turn it into a story. So maybe it doesn’t matter that the subject of the picture isn’t actually Paz Pardo de Tavera. If it means people remember her story and, by extension, the story of so many women whose meaningless murders people thought were justified?
Maybe that’s the very meaning of the term “print the legend.”
Manchester man successfully flies to Spain on Ryanair flight using his wife’s passport
You get what you pay for.
A man flew from Manchester to Spain for a stag party using his wife’s passport by mistake, something that wasn’t flagged by staff at Manchester Airport.

Ben Moore told BBC Radio Stoke that the mix-up was only revealed when he touched down in Alicante and began queueing up for passport control. In the interview, he said, “I opened up the passport there and, to my horror, it was my wife’s photo on the passport.”
He then said, “I searched through all my luggage about eight times thinking there’s no way I could have got to Alicante without my own passport.”
Moore initially thought that he’d picked up both by mistake, used his own to get through customs back in Manchester before taking out the other one in Spain.

After all, Moore owns property in Spain and makes the trip multiple times a year. It was possible that he’d made a mistake while on autopilot. However, he realised that the only passport he had in his luggage belonged to his wife. Something that confused Spanish authorities just as much as him after he went to them and explained the situation. A process that Moore said the police officers there were “a little bit intimidating” about.

Moore’s trip ended early, with him being put straight back on a flight to the UK while his friends continued the stag party without him. The flight out from Manchester was operated by Ryanair, who have announced that they’ll be reviewing the matter.
However, they also stated that passenger document checks at the boarding gate are technically not carried out by the company themselves, but by their third-party ground handling provider Swissport.

BBC News reached out to Manchester Airport for comment, who said that the responsibility for checking passports lies with the airlines, as airports only ask for boarding cards from passengers when passing through security.
Nobody’s Ever Asked Me That : Anna Konkle
The co-creator/co-star of Pen15 , whose beautiful memoir The Sane One came out earlier this year, gets deep on therapy, childhood trauma and ill-advised travel.
My guest today is actor, comedian and writer Anna Konkle, whose excellent memoir The Sane One cameout earlier this year.

If you know Konkle from anything, it’s almost certainly Pen15 , the TV show she co-created and co-starred in with Maya Erskine , in which the thirtysomething pair played awkward 12-year-old best friends navigating the perils of middle-school life, acting opposite real tweens.
Konkle and Erskine mined their own respective adolescences to create an inspired comedy that was hilarious and painful in equal measure, and rightly became a cultural phenomenon.

Straight after Konkle finished the second and final season of Pen15 , she began writing The Sane One , which looks at her life through the lens of childhood trauma and the shadow it has cast over her adulthood.

Though there are moments of humor, The Sane One is not one of those light comedic memoirs. Instead, the book is emotionally incredibly acute and insightful, as Konkle details her mother’s mental health issues and her complex relationship with her father, from whom she was estranged for five years, reconciling only shortly before his death. The book also shows the extensive work Konkle has done on herself to process the pain of the past and find empathy for the people in her life, with that growth best exemplified by a remarkable letter she wrote to her father.

My conversation with Konkle was beset by some technical issues, but if anything it kinda bonded us as we talked about such diverse topics as: why each of us tells white lies, her (sometimes reckless) quest for adventure in the Himalayas, how to navigate eating alone, re-evaluating her childhood after watching an old home movie, how Pen15 was essentially a $20 million therapy session, why Al-Anon needs to get the Raya treatment, and much more.
The Sane Out is now wherever you get your books, and it’s terrific. I’ll give a special recommendation to the audiobook, and if you haven’t seen Pen15 , you should go check it out ASAP.

What do 35 years of touring the UK look like to Manic Street Preachers?
Here’s what Nicky Wire remembers best, as told to The Quietus editor John Doran. An excerpt from issue one of SHOWNOTES.

I am very much a homebird, so when it came time for Manic Street Preachers to go on tour I was nervous about it. My Dad had an old grandad’s chair, which he managed to tie to the wall in the back of the hire van, so someone could have a seat on the way to the gig. It was incredibly dangerous. And then on the way back, James would just get in a sleeping bag and lie down in the back of the van, rolling around all over the place as we were driving back home. He can sleep anywhere.

We had such a deep bonding experience on the Motown Junk Tour in 1991. The staff at the venues were just so friendly; you felt that they really cared. I remember getting to the Stoke Wheatsheaf – a magical venue – and we hadn’t had any food for a day and a half. They made us the most beautiful burger and chips.

King Tut’s Wah Wah Hut, Glasgow? The Stoker, Coventry? The Barrel Organ, Birmingham? JB’s, Dudley? Moles, Bath? The Adelphi, Hull? The Leadmill, Sheffield? It was a truly magical tour, I can’t even remember any bad shows.

The greatest one was probably The Buzz Club in Aldershot. What a fucking venue. Who’d have thought if you were in a rock band, going to Aldershot would give you one of the greatest gigs of your life? It was full of squaddies because it’s an army town, and it was antagonistic, but also brilliant. That was on the edge but some gigs could tip over the edge.

We did quite a scary gig at Reading’s After Dark Club. There was a proper firm of football hooligans there. That film The Firm had just been on TV and I don’t know if it had got people excited but it kicked off. James got punched but we stood our ground. There was a real adrenaline rush to it, even if there was a hint of violence at a lot of those early gigs.

What strikes me now is that all of these places were towns and I wonder how many of them have that kind of gig venue left. You can still play gigs in the cities, but to play in these towns was amazing: learning your trade and meeting people. Also realising there are people like you in every town you go to.

Very early doors, Little Chefs were different – they deserve an honourable mention because you could just get a proper meal there. A plate of bacon, egg and chips. We loved going to them but even by the time we started touring they were getting harder to find. And in the services before they improved, all you could find was some dodgy pasty that had been sitting in a fridge for weeks. But I have a theory that bad food equals great music. Show me a band that’s eaten healthy food all of their lives and their music is always shit. Whereas The Fall, those bands in Seattle that just lived on hard drugs and strong coffee, Sex Pistols… they lived on bad motorway service station diets and they made the greatest music. I think if you care that much about your bodily health, you’re shutting off a pathway to creativity.

C.O.F.F.I.N time! Where on earth do I begin? Opening the set with Out In Oslo caused the room to erupt and it pretty much stayed like that for the whole time. I love everything that C.O.F.F.I.N stand for, and whilst the night was ridiculously fun- they used their platform to highlight the domestic violence rates in Australia, how corrupt governments are, calling people out on their shitty behaviours and not make life harder for those of us in marginalised communities. How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

Last Tuesday I went to Paris for my birthday. I came home yesterday, and I miss it. I miss friendliness, everything feeling slower, good vegan food, sleeping in a bed that doesn’t hurt my back and a decent shower. It was the perfect way to see off my 30s, and the last band I saw of my 30s on the day before my birthday was Penelope Isles.

What made the show special is that Lily, Jack and I are from the Isle of Man. I felt like a piece of home was in the room on Wednesday night and there were times where I was trying to not cry a little. It’s weird because I have such a weird relationship with the Isle of Man, but that’s not for here. That’s for elsewhere.

I’ve only been to gigs in the UK but I can honestly say that the crowd at Supersonic were just lovely, and it was a joy to be in such a beautiful environment. People were respectful of personal space and there were no drunken idiots ruining it for everyone. Although the set was just under an hour; it was a perfect set. Every song was delivered in such a perfect and tender way. You felt every song, and connected with every word. The set opened with 3, and it was straight into Thinking Seat which just hits you right in the soul and all feels okay. For me, it was Birthdays that did it. That song very nearly got tears out of me (it’s been a comfort) and to see it live was such a gorgeous moment, and it makes you appreciate the song and the record in general, even more so when you see it live. Another Kind Of Love shows just how delicate Jack’s vocals are, and where there are moments in the set where Jack, Lily and Joe absolutely tear the roof off the venue (especially during Gnarbone, which was an insane way to end the show)- you just really see how bloody talented this band is, and they truly deserve the world.

The room felt like it was filled with love and just appreciation for the band, and maybe it was extra special because it was the last night of the tour, but it just felt like one of those shows that people will talk about in years to come and those of us who were there will know exactly how lucky we were. It was a truly stunning show, and is up there as being one of my favourites of the year. Lily, Jack and Joe are just exceptional musicians, and it was a real honour to witness their greatness last week. I also felt super proud that a band from where I’m from are playing venues like Supersonic and just being a dream to watch.

At the end of the show, my partner and I went up to the merch stand and Lily spotted my Bushy’s t-shirt. I told her I was from the Isle of Man, and it was one of the most wholesome moments I’ve had. Jack and I had our photo taken together, with our Bushy’s shirts, and spoke about home for a little bit. It was nice to have a piece of home and to meet the band who have again, released one of the best records of the year.

If you’ve not listened to 3 yet, I urge you to do so. There is so much love, loss, thought, care and heart on the record and when you witness it live- you hear the record differently. The bond between Jack and Lily is so beautiful, and you just feel so lucky to witness the greatness of all 3 of them on stage together. At times the songs are mellow and soothing, and there are other moments in the set where this gorgeous loudness takes over. Ending the set with Gnarbone was just heaven! Opening or closing with it was always going to be magic!

Another Kind Of Love going into Birthdays then into Moonwalker was a piece of musical heaven. I honestly couldn’t have wished for a better band to say bye bye to my 30s to (I saw Fontaines D.C the day after my birthday on Friday, so I really have lucked out here!)
It’s pretty fair to say that Penny Isles show is truly special, and you take what you need from it. It’ll make you wish you could watch them every night in Paris. Everything is better in Paris.
(There’s another cool photo of us on the Penny Isles Instagram too!)
