The new single by PINS, No More Tears is beautiful. And if you want to truly feel the beauty of the song and soak up the vulnerability of the lyrics- then watch the music videos. PINS have always made stunning music videos, but the one for No More Tears has a real sense of community, love, friendship, some loss, healing, and honesty. No More Tears is a real tender moment, and it almost feels like a lullaby. Maybe it is. Maybe it’s a lullaby with added bite. Honestly, this is PINS at their very best. It’s such a dreamy, blissed-out song with their signature touch; how could you not become obsessed with this gem of a song! I will talk about this band (and many others) to anyone who will listen, and I think this could be my go to PINS song if someone hasn’t heard them before. Start with this, and prepare to have your mind blown and your heart stolen.

I say it every single time, but that’s because PINS are consistently great, however this again just shows how fantastic the band are. Lyrically, musically, vocally- everything. The video is dedicated to their friend Em, and adding something so precious to the end of the video makes you appreciate the song even more. Grief is a thief and we face it however and whatever way we can. Thank goodness we have music. Will I cry when they do this live? Of course. I cry too much, ha!

No More Tears has no resemblance to any thing PINS have done before but fits perfectly in with the songs they’ve released from the new record to date, and I think that’s pretty much setting us up for a strong contender for the best record of 2027. I cannot wait for the new record, and they are playing some special shows to coincide with the release. I’ve seen them nearing 20 odd times I think now, and this will be my first time seeing them in Manchester. I have no idea how it’s taken me so long, but I cannot wait.

The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. Victory can be earned on points – the three judges look for clean technique and the impact a strike makes – but about half are won via knockout. The podium is padded, as the competitors sometimes collide with it on the way down. Behind each competitor stand two catchers to grab them as they fall. When Power Slap introduced a super-heavyweight division, where contestants can weigh the same as an upright piano, they hired professional strongmen for the job.

More than 200,000 Carbon Monoxide Detectors Are Being Recalled Due to the Risk of “Serious Injury or…
Around 210,000 carbon monoxide detectors are being recalled because they don't properly detect dangerous levels of carbon monoxide.

Some recalls are more serious than others, and this is a serious one. More than 210,000 carbon monoxide and natural gas detectors are being recalled because they can fail to alert consumers to dangerous levels of carbon monoxide , potentially putting people at risk of serious injury or death.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) announced the recall on Wednesday, Nov. 25, involving Steadfast Haven 4-in-1 plug-in CO and natural gas detectors sold by Zenara Commerce LLC.
What consumers need to know about the recall
So, how do you know if you have an affected device? Here’s the scoop.

The recall covers models KH158 and GC03, with approximately 210,410 units affected. The KH158 model is round in shape. It comes in gray or white plastic housing with a black digital display. Meanwhile, the GC03 model is rectangular with a black housing and a black digital display. Consumers can find the model number on the white label on the back of the device, right near the plug.
Consumers purchased the detectors online at Truststeadfast.com between February 2026 and September 2026. They cost around $48 to $70.

The biggest concern is that these devices may not sound an alarm when hazardous levels of carbon monoxide are present. Carbon monoxide is particularly dangerous because it is odorless and colorless, making a functioning detector an important safety device in the home.
According to the CPSC, Zenara has received one report of a detector failing to alarm during a carbon monoxide leak. No injuries have been reported, however.

Consumers should contact Zenara immediately to request a free replacement. The company is asking customers to register at www.truststeadfast.com/pages/recall , mark the recalled detector with the word “RECALLED” and their initials using permanent marker, then upload a photo of the marked product.
Consumers should continue using their recalled detectors until the replacement is installed. Once registration is confirmed, they should dispose of the recalled unit in their household trash.

For additional information, consumers can email recall@truststeadfast.com or visit the company’s recall website. Given the potential consequences, this is one recall homeowners won’t want to overlook.

Consumer Product Safety Commission : “Zenara Recalls 4-in-1 Plug in Steadfast Haven Carbon Monoxide (CO) and Natural Gas Detectors Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Failure to Alert Consumers to Hazardous Levels of Gas and CO”
Patrick Stewart Pushed Through Health Struggles to Film Avengers: Doomsday—And It Was “Intensely Emotional”
The Russo Brothers said Patrick Stewart persevered through health struggles to deliver his final performance as Professor Xavier.
Patrick Stewart gave his final performance everything he had.

Nearly a month after the beloved actor’s death at age 86, Avengers: Doomsday directors Joe and Anthony Russo opened up about what it was like working with Stewart as he reprised his iconic role of Professor Charles Xavier one last time.

The upcoming Marvel blockbuster, which hits theaters Dec. 18, will mark Stewart’s final onscreen performance. And according to the Russo brothers, the actor’s dedication to his craft was particularly moving given the health challenges he was facing behind the scenes.
Patrick Stewart’s health struggles made filming Avengers: Doomsday especially emotional

Speaking with Entertainment Weekly in a piece shared Nov. 24, Anthony recalled how determined Stewart was to give his fellow cast and crew members the best possible experience despite his declining health. “It was clear that he was struggling with his health, and he worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence—for us as directors, for his other actors, for the crew,” Anthony said.

The director explained that Stewart’s commitment went far beyond what was typically expected of an actor arriving on set. “For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional.”

Stewart’s final day of filming also included a memorable speech to the cast and crew. Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige recalled that the actor seemed aware it might be his last time on a movie set. “He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew,” Feige said. “We didn’t know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was.”
Marvel is looking for a way to honor Patrick Stewart
Stewart’s family announced his death on Oct. 29, revealing that the actor had died from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia .

Although Marvel initially offered Stewart roles in both Avengers: Doomsday and its 2027 sequel, Avengers: Secret Wars , he opted to appear only in the former. His final performance will also feature an emotional scene about forgiveness opposite longtime friend and fellow X-Men star Ian McKellen, who returns as Magneto.
Feige confirmed that Marvel is currently exploring ways to commemorate Stewart in the upcoming film. “We’re looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend.”

Like the time I dropped a baking dish of perfectly browned, crispy-edged roasted potatoes on my tile floor, or the time—or, should I say, times?—I ran out of ice. Because here’s the thing: Holiday-party disasters are inevitable. You can plan for every possible scenario, but eventually something will go sideways. And when it does, well, the party must go on.

The trick is knowing how to recover without turning a minor snafu into a major production. As event planner Renee Patrone Rhinehart puts it, “Your guests probably have no idea something went wrong until you start announcing it to everyone.” Her advice? “Just roll with it!”

To find out how to roll with a dozen of the most common holiday-party disasters when you’re hosting , I went to the experts. Iron Chef Alex Guarnaschelli and renowned Southern chef Carla Hall weigh in on turkey troubles and other food emergencies; event planners Rhinehart and Marcy Blum share their secrets for keeping a party on track; etiquette expert Myka Meier offers advice for navigating awkward social situations; and licensed marriage and family therapist Nari Jeter, PhD, weighs in on emotionally charged moments.

So whether your turkey is taking forever to cook, an unexpected guest arrives or your uncle decides today is the perfect time to reignite that family feud, here’s how to save the celebration—and your sanity. Party on!

You’re still getting dressed, the kitchen is a disaster zone, and the appetizers aren’t even out yet. Then the doorbell rings—20 minutes before you expected anyone. Now you need to switch into host mode, and fast.

What to do: Welcome them warmly, offer a drink , and, if you’re comfortable, give them a small task, like putting on the music or lighting candles. “You’re early! Perfect timing. Grab a drink, and help me finish up!” is a perfectly acceptable response, says Rhinehart. My friends know that’s the case at my house: You show up early, and I’m putting you to work.

(For what it’s worth: Meier notes that guests should arrive at the stated time for a seated dinner; for a more casual gathering, arriving 10 to 15 minutes after the start time is generally appropriate.)

Why it works: You don’t need to drop everything to entertain an early arrival. A little hospitality goes a long way, and giving someone a simple job can make them feel included rather than in the way. It can even turn into a bonding moment with your new guest!

You planned dinner for eight, set the table for eight and made just enough food for eight. Then someone shows up with an unexpected plus-one. You could panic about the extra chair and plate, or you could get creative and make it work.

What to do: Take a breath , pull up an extra chair and welcome that person as though you expected them all along. “As a host, your goal is to make everyone feel welcome, even when you’re caught off guard,” says Meier. Simply say, “How lovely to meet you! Come on in.” After all, she adds, “It was not the guest’s fault they were asked to be there, and you don’t want them to feel that when arriving.”

Blum says to have card stock and a pen on hand to make an extra place card, if necessary. Rhinehart recommends stretching the meal with whatever you have—bread, salad or an extra side—and resisting the urge to announce that you weren’t prepared for another person.

Why it works: You’re taking charge, being an excellent hostess and rolling with the surprise. Making a fuss, on the other hand, can turn a small logistical hiccup into an awkward moment. As Rhinehart says, “Nobody needs to know!”

Is It Really Rude to Opt Out of the Gift Exchange?
The anxiety—and financial pressure—of getting a present for a group gift swap can feel exhausting during an already overscheduled season. Can you just skip it? The post Is It Really Rude to…

Like all torturous extended family traditions, ours started with good intentions. One year, someone got left off the list during our chaotic annual Christmas gift free-for-all. Feelings were hurt. So being responsible adults, we fixed the problem by inventing an entire bureaucracy: the Official Family Gift Exchange.

The idea was fine. The rules were what ruined us. It started with just drawing names. Then we added a price limit. Then a price minimum, after somebody’s “gift” turned out to be an already-opened bottle of lotion. Then a rule requiring you to talk to your assigned person about their interests, which metastasized into a 15-question survey, then into a shared spreadsheet, tracked with the rigor of a Pentagon budget.

Then the “ no regifting ” clause. Then the Great Gift Card Debate, which raged for years: Do gift cards even count as real gifts? Does one to a specific store outrank a Visa card? Does it have to be taped to something ­wrappable, or are we now just handing each other receipts?

It all came to a head the year my husband’s gift got returned to him. Not regifted— returned, like a defective toaster , with a note that it wasn’t thoughtful enough. Being an eternal optimist, he tried again. That gift also came back, this time via USPS, meaning the recipient paid actual postage to send it away rather than keep it one more day. That’s when we knew we wanted out. It wasn’t working anymore.

My husband and I decided to pull the plug. No elaborate exchange, just a gift card to each family, no survey required. What had started as a fun, generous tradition had somehow turned into a monthlong hostage situation that began every November.

Naturally, quitting had consequences: The following year, someone anonymously (although I’m pretty sure I know who) sent us a calendar of dogs pooping. (Yes, that’s a thing. And yes, you can buy it. I do not recommend gifting it, though I also cannot stop thinking about the person who decided the world needed it as a wall calendar.)

It’s not just my family that has a hard time managing this. More often than not, gift exchanges—office, family or friend group—start as a fun idea but end up being a spreadsheet with hurt feelings. So is opting out of the whole enterprise actually rude?

Financially, gift exchanges have quietly inflated like everything else. A $10 white elephant gag gift is now a $25-and-up “guideline” that creeps to $40 the second someone brings a nice candle. Multiply that by the office exchange, the neighborhood exchange and the family swaps, and you’re out $200 before buying anything for someone you actually live with. And, it must be said, in this economy?

There are also the plain logistics: Exchanges take time most of us don’t have in December. Saying no to one more obligation isn’t a personality flaw; it’s functioning boundaries. And if the group’s response to “I’ll sit this one out” is outrage, that says more about their expectations than your manners.

If only it were that easy. Gift swaps, especially the family and friend kind, aren’t really about the gift. They’re a shared ritual , and rituals only work if everyone shows up. Opt out and you can shift the whole dynamic—an odd number of ornaments, a recalculated spreadsheet, or Grandma noticing the empty spot under the tree and asking about it at dinner, forever.

There’s also the momentum problem. Once one person opts out “just this year,” the tradition can quietly die. If the exchange genuinely matters to the group, your exit—however ­reasonable—can be the beginning of the end for people who looked forward to it.

Context is everything, and office, family and friend exchanges are not all the same animal. Office exchanges are the easiest to skip—it’s a workplace, not a family reunion, and “I’m sitting this one out” needs zero explanation. Unless, of course, your boss makes it mandatory.

In contemplating the theory of general relativity, Albert Einstein imagined a falling lift in which people are performing experiments :

One of the observers takes a handkerchief and a watch from his pocket and drops them. What happens to these two bodies? … [F]or the outside observer they are both falling with the same acceleration. But so is the lift, with its walls, ceiling, and floor. Therefore: the distance between the two bodies and the floor will not change.

This notion of the equivalence between gravity and acceleration, which he called “the happiest thought of my life,” came to Einstein in 1907. Interestingly, Lewis Carroll had explored a similar scenario in 1889:
‘One can easily imagine a situation,’ said Arthur, ‘where things would necessarily have no weight, relatively to each other, though each would have its usual weight, looked at by itself.’
‘Some desperate paradox!’ said the Earl. ‘Tell us how it could be. We shall never guess it.’
‘Well, suppose this house, just as it is, placed a few billion miles above a planet, and with nothing else near enough to disturb it: of course it falls to the planet?’
The Earl nodded. ‘Of course — though it might take some centuries to do it.’
‘And is five-o’clock-tea to be going on all the while?’ said Lady Muriel.

‘That, and other things,’ said Arthur. ‘The inhabitants would live their lives, grow up and die, and still the house would be falling, falling, falling! But now as to the relative weight of things. Nothing can be heavy , you know, except by trying to fall, and being prevented from doing so. You all grant that?’

‘Well, now, if I take this book, and hold it out at arm’s length, of course I feel its weight . It is trying to fall, and I prevent it. And, if I let go, it falls to the floor. But, if we were all falling together, it couldn’t be trying to fall any quicker, you know: for, if I let go, what more could it do than fall? And, as my hand would be falling too — at the same rate — it would never leave it, for that would be to get ahead of it in the race. And it could never overtake the falling floor!’

What is the Holiday Wish Line?

First launched in December 2023, the Holiday Wish Line features prerecorded messages from children who have had their wishes granted by Make-A-Wish. Think jokes, holiday songs, personal stories and the kind of words of encouragement that somehow hit differently when they come from a kid.
This year, the hotline opened on Nov. 23, just in time for the Thanksgiving rush . Anyone nationwide can call (480) 914-9474 (WISH) through Dec. 31.

Meet the kids on the other end of the line

Angelito celebrated his fifth birthday in style with a traditional Mexican charro party, complete with live music, presents and horses.
Braedyn got to lace up a pair of ice skates and glide around the rink for the very first time.
Deon traded South Florida sunshine for a snowy Vermont getaway, where dozens of people surprised him with an epic snowball fight.

Here’s How to Easily Record Your Entire Family History So No One Forgets Who’s Who in All Those Photos
Up to your eyeballs in old photos, letters and records? These expert tips to document your family history will help you organize everything and connect the dots.

My sister and I were recently hanging out at her place, and the conversation turned to our childhood. I pulled up some old photos on my phone—snaps of pictures that used to live in albums at the center of my parents’ living room. We started taking guesses about when they were from and shared stories about what was happening in them. We both remembered family picnics at the waterfall, our dog Cujo (yes, Cujo), and flying kites in the cornfield across the house. But there were people, places and stories I couldn’t recall at all, like a close family friend’s house we spent a lot of time at; my sister could still describe it in detail.
That’s when it hit me: It had been years since we’d flipped through old albums like that. As physical albums get left behind and older relatives depart, we’re increasingly losing our family history.

I’ve researched bits of my family’s genealogy over the years, but I’ve always run into roadblocks. Like many families in the U.S., our ancestors immigrated several generations ago, and a lot of details were lost or changed along the way. How do you document family history when there are so many missing pieces? By tackling it little by little, says Allison Singleton, the genealogy services manager at the Genealogy Center. “There will be gaps of information you don’t know,” she says. But don’t let that stop you.

That being said, you’ll have a lot more luck if you have a method to the madness. That’s why I reached out to a few experts who do this for a living and could lay it out in simple terms for us. In addition to Singleton, I spoke with Kyle Betit, a senior genealogist at Ancestry; Haleh Shoa, a certified professional photo organizer and the founder of Picturli; and Peter Andrew Wint, the founder of Family Roots.

It turns out, there are a lot of strategies and resources available, and some of them are free. Read on to find out how to document family history , create a family tree and be the detective your clan needs—starting now!
How on earth do you even start this kind of project?
Before you dive into documenting your family’s history, determine your goal. “Knowing where you want to end up tells you where to start and how much you need to gather,” Shoa says.

Next, collect supplies. Shoa says you’ll need several plastic bins, colorful index cards for categorizing batches of photos, an archival pencil, a 2TB or 4TB external hard drive for storage, nitrile gloves for handling photos, and a notebook or spreadsheet for tracking.

Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. Think of this like taking an inventory. “Put like with like,” Shoa says. “The albums, the slides, the negatives and the VHS tapes should each have their own piles.” In addition to photos and videos, include things like old letters , newspaper clippings, obituaries, birth and death certificates, and recipe cards. “These items are full of clues about your family history,” Singleton notes. After you’ve grouped everything, you’ll dig into each category. (More on that below.)

Keep in mind that you don’t need to do everything at once. “Start small—with one photograph, one document, one family story, one person or one question—and see how your research progresses,” Singleton advises. After all, you don’t want to get overwhelmed before you even really start!
How do you create a family tree?
To create a family tree, gather and cross-check details about your family, and designate a place to keep it all organized. Follow these steps to get started.
Building your tree online allows you to save and share it virtually, and on some platforms, you can turn on collaborative permissions so relatives can contribute in real time.

If you’re looking for a free and simple platform that’s particularly good for beginners, Shoa recommends Family Echo. You can also create a basic free tree in FamilySearch, Canva, Ancestry and MyHeritage. Just be aware that free trees may have limitations, and access to some records and services may require a paid subscription.

How to Navigate Grief During the Holidays in Ways You’ll Actually Find Helpful
When the season feels anything but merry, these expert tips will give you a game plan to make it through—even when that feels impossible.

No matter what time of year you’ve lost someone, navigating that grief during the season devoted to joy, togetherness and sparkle can become a challenge unto itself. When my 82-year-old mom died the night before Thanksgiving three years ago, my grief became permanently imprinted into the holidays. Ever since, I’ve swung between wanting to eat cookies by the fire with Santa and scream through the streets with Krampus.

The holidays haven’t felt the same since, and admittedly, I even feel a little dread around this time of the year. I’m not alone. According to American Psychiatric Association’s Healthy Minds poll from 2025 about holiday-related concerns, nearly half of adults polled felt worry over grief and missing someone . The reality is that the best parts of the season can lead to some of the worst feelings of loss.

There is no easy answer here, unfortunately, but experts do have a few suggestions to help people handle grief during the holidays . For that advice, I spoke with Raman Mohabir, PhD, a licensed professional clinical counselor and the founder of Good Mourning Mental Health Counseling, and Tess Clarkson, an end-of-life doula and the creator of the Your Best Goodbye workshop.
Read on to find out how to get through the holidays after a loss , find special ways to honor your loved ones and maybe even enjoy the season again.
Why are the holidays particularly hard after a loss?

First of all, it’s not your imagination: The holidays are harder. And the first notes of a familiar holiday song or the scent of a special dish can really feel like a gut punch. “The holiday season can further magnify grief because it is a time often marked with moments meant to be spent with family and loved ones, which can further highlight the absence of the person who has died,” Mohabir says . On top of that, you may feel guilt, anger or resentment for not feeling celebratory, and your grief can feel darker against all the sparkle.

How it hits can also depend on the kind of loss. Grief isn’t only about death, Mohabir notes. It can also include “ambiguous losses, such as the anticipatory grief associated with the decline of a loved one facing a terminal diagnosis, or loss due to divorce, deployment, incarceration or a miscarriage.” Those losses can be especially lonely during the holidays. “These ambiguous and disenfranchised grief experiences can complicate the holiday season as well, especially if the loss is not acknowledged or supported by others,” she says.
Whatever kind of loss you’re carrying, feeling as if you’re living a different holiday than everyone around you can be alienating.
Should you still celebrate the holidays after a loss?

It really depends on you. “There is no correct answer or moral obligation to how an individual should navigate the holiday season,” says Mohabir. A lot of it boils down to how you feel and who will be around you . Spending time with people who share your loss, or who are simply supportive, can be a real comfort and worth the effort. Spending it with people who aren’t supportive can do more harm than good, whether they’re friends or family.

“It is important to assess the quality of the support around you and what you need when gathering with others,” Mohabir says. Time alone counts too. “Choosing solitude and privacy can be restorative and healing as well,” she adds.

If celebrating feels like too much this year, try a gentler approach: “observing” the season or focusing on getting through it rather than celebrating it. “Maybe it is not putting up the tree or getting out the menorah,” Clarkson says. It’s also not all or nothing; Show up for dessert, pop by Christmas morning—”it’s about having more serenity without the performance of the holidays,” she says.
How should you approach the holiday season after a loss?

Start by listening to yourself rather than to your list of obligations. There’s no single right way to do the holidays while grieving. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all,” Clarkson says. “It behooves us to listen to ourselves for what we need.” That might be a walk, a good cry or a quiet night in, she says, or it might be more appointments with the therapist or a grief support group.

This Junk-Drawer Staple Could Save Your Home in Case of Flooding, According to a New Study
A new study found that a surprisingly effective and cheap household tool blows sandbags out of the water when it comes to flood protection.

Flooding often brings to mind springtime thunderstorms and late-summer hurricanes, but this year, El Niño is serving up a nasty winter across much of the United States. Heavy rains and flooding are in the forecast for huge swaths of the country, leaving many wondering what they would do if water was bearing down.

Sandbags have been the go-to for centuries, but if you’ve ever tried to use them, you know they are a pain: heavy, labor-intensive and often not available when you need them. But now, researchers looking for inexpensive ways to help homeowners fight flooding have stumbled across something that blows sandbags out of the water.

Britain’s University of Hull released the surprising findings in a new report, and we have the results ahead. It turns out that something you no doubt have rattling around in your junk drawer or garage toolbox works better than sandbags—a lot better. Read on to learn an effective (and cheap) way to protect your home during a flood.
What junk-drawer staple can save your home from flooding?

That’s according to a new report called Testing the Performance of Low-cost, Temporary Property Flood Resilience (PFR) Solutions . The university teamed up with Flood Re, a partnership between the U.K. government and insurers, to pinpoint inexpensive ways for homeowners to protect their homes during a flood.

The results were amazing: Duct tape reduced water leakage 97% to 98% compared to a plain closed door. The much less common synthetic rubber tape (aka putty tape) did even better, with a 99% reduction. Even the worst-performing tape, yellow plastic tape, kept out 80% of simulated floodwaters during testing. And every single tape tested did better than sandbags, which reduced water intrusion by only 70%.

“Sandbags remain a symbol of flood protection , but these tests turn that assumption on its head,” said Jonathan Kassian, head of flood resilience at Flood Re. “What we have found is that some relatively simple and affordable products can do a much better job of keeping water out.”
Why does this work better than a sandbag?

For one thing, sandbags are porous, and they’re not designed to keep out water completely. Think of them more as a diversion tactic or obstruction, as opposed to tape, which can actually seal an opening through which water can flow.

In this study, researchers found that when placed in flood conditions of 0.2 meters (about 8 inches), sandbags leaked water at a mean rate of 584 liters per hour per meter, or 47 gallons per hour per foot. They were more effective in deeper water, but still only prevented, at most, 70% of water leakage . Sandbags are also heavy, time-intensive to deploy and difficult to place correctly.

Tape, on the other hand, is cheap and easy to store. It can be applied directly across gaps and conforms to irregular surfaces and openings where water can seep in. After the storm, cleanup is easy because tape is safely disposable, unlike sandbags, which absorb dangerous floodwater contaminants. And remember: Duct tape was more than 97% effective.
There is one caveat. Researchers concluded that how the tape was applied was “critical.” We’ll give you those details next.
How do you do this properly?

First, it’s important to understand that this was a research study about the effectiveness of certain barriers under testing conditions, not a how-to manual of using tape to stop a flood. But scientists were encouraged by the findings. Here are recommendations from the report:
Use a strong, wide tape. For duct tape, researchers recommend a width of 100 mm (roughly 4 inches).
Apply it to the flood-facing side. Tape performed best when it was applied on the outside of the door.

Cover vertical joints first. Tape the sides, making sure the vertical strip is attached to both the door and jamb and extends to the threshold. Then do the threshold and corners, overlapping the vertical strip.
Apply to clean, dry doors. To get the best adhesion, tape the door before wet weather arrives .
Make sure there are no openings. Avoid folds, press out any air bubbles and cover gaps.

This essay is co-published with Vittles and appears in Vittles Issue No. 3: The Influencers .
Vaughn Tan | Longreads | November 24, 2026 | 3,989 words (17 minutes)

Back in 2003, I was in the early stages of researching how the distinctive visual style of Japanese plating and dish design influenced plating outside Japan, and wanted to analyze photos of fine-dining dishes in industry periodicals like Art Culinaire . Back in the early 2000s, this was easiest to do in libraries. At the time, I lived in Cambridge, Massachusetts, so I wound up in the collection of historical cookbooks and culinary materials at the Schlesinger Library.

One afternoon, Barbara Haber, then the Schlesinger’s curator of books, stopped by my desk with something for me: Japanese Cooking: A Simple Art by Shizuo Tsuji, published in 1980 with an introduction by MFK Fisher. I knew of Fisher through her essays on eating and her translation of Brillat-Savarin’s The Physiology of Taste , but not for anything related to Japanese food. Barbara mentioned that many boxes of Fisher’s collected papers had recently arrived at the library. The papers were still uncatalogued, but was I interested in looking at them?

I didn’t know then that I was beginning a 20-year detour. As I went through these boxes over the next few months, my original research project faded away. I found myself more and more drawn to the Fisher archive boxes, and to the story that emerged as I read through years of her correspondence and other documents, including letters about her trip to Japan to research the introduction she wrote to Japanese Cooking ; letters about the book she wrote to journalists, writers, and editors across the US; and draft manuscripts of Japanese Cooking , with her comments in red pen, which had crisscrossed the Pacific between California and Osaka. The story that emerged was of a secret campaign Fisher waged between 1979 and 1982, which was instrumental in the seemingly sudden transformation of Japanese food into fine dining in America.
The Fisher I uncovered in those boxes was someone else, and her role in making Japanese food into fine dining in America remains almost entirely unknown.

Fisher’s campaign worked well because it was largely invisible. The publishers of Japanese Cooking didn’t know that any of this was happening. Ruth Reichl, who wrote the foreword to the 25th anniversary edition in 2005, had no idea Fisher had done any more than write the introduction when I spoke to her earlier this year. (Fisher had gifted her a copy of the book before Reichl’s first trip to Japan in the early 1980s.) Yet Fisher not only shaped the book itself, she also systematically put it in front of everyone who mattered in the American food world—people whose endorsement could not be bought, and whose reasons for endorsing the book were, as I later realized, largely Fisher’s own.

In 2003, I wasn’t sure what to do with my discovery. It didn’t fit any story I knew how to tell yet. And although it made sense to me back then that no one had uncovered this evidence before—Fisher’s campaign was visible only through forensic analysis of an uncatalogued archive, and left no traces in the places people normally look—in the years since, it has remained largely unexamined, even though Fisher is an extensively examined writer. Her reputation has grown considerably over the past two decades and, in the UK especially, she is now frequently invoked as the great American food writer.
But the Fisher I uncovered in those boxes was someone else, and her role in making Japanese food into fine dining in America remains almost entirely unknown. This is what she did.

Until the late 1970s, Japanese food wasn’t just exotic to the American public, it was fundamentally alien. That Sinking Feeling: A Race Against Time to Save a Pregnant Woman from a Car Submerged in Freezing Waters
A dazed pregnant woman drives into an ice-cold pond. Amid a sea of bystanders, one man takes action to save her life.

Shedly Apollon was awakened by a sound she couldn’t possibly sleep through: that of her car splashing into a pond … with her in it. Add in the rush of cold water pooling beneath her feet, and suddenly Apollon was fully alert, if disoriented. She was also fearing for her life. Actually, two lives. Apollon was in her 34th week of pregnancy on that cold morning this past February in Stuart, Florida, when she awoke to the reality that she was trapped in a sinking car .

Apollon, of nearby Port St. Lucie, had been on her way to a prenatal massage gifted by her fiancé, Woodly Sully. It was a birthday present. (Yes, this happened on Apollon’s 29th birthday.) Apollon had been struggling during her third trimester with preeclampsia, and as she drove to the massage, she began to feel woozy. She pulled her silver 2019 Hyundai Elantra over to the shoulder of Interstate 95, called Sully to let him know what was happening, drank some water, ate a little food and waited for the dizziness to subside.

After it did, about 10 minutes later, she got back on the road, but what happened next is a blur. Her car’s safety systems were beeping, telling her she was veering outside her lane, although in her haze-filled mind she was driving perfectly straight. She tried to pull over again, but started passing out. “I thought the car was in park,” Apollon recalls, “but in reality, it was still in drive.” And she drove off the right side of the road, straight into the pond.

When she came to seconds later to the sound of the splash, she unsnapped her seat belt and hit redial on her phone, then screamed to her confused fiancé, “I’m in a lake!” Within seconds, the call dropped. She and her unborn baby were all alone in a car that was listing, front driver’s side first, into a body of water.

Around this time, 29-year-old sport fisherman Logan Hayes of Sebastian, Florida, was driving down the same stretch of I-95 in his pickup, remarking to his friend and boss in the passenger seat, Chase Cornell, about how unusual it was that traffic was light and that they were running 20 minutes ahead of schedule on their work errand. “Something’s gonna happen,” Hayes joked.
Sure enough, Hayes soon saw brake lights ahead of him. And then the reason for the sudden slowdown: the Elantra, barely floating in the water.

Other cars had pulled over, but so far nobody had gotten out to help. So Hayes, also a professional surfer and confident swimmer, crossed from the far left lane across two other lanes, cutting off every car in his way, then pulled onto the shoulder and leaped out of the truck.
“Hey, is someone in that car?” he asked a bystander.

Hayes ran 50 yards down the highway, then a few more feet to the water’s edge, his eyes fixed on the Elantra. He was shedding clothing every step of the way. Off came his hat, his sunglasses, his shirt, his fishing boots, his sweatpants, his socks … until all he had on were his board shorts.

The outdoor temperature was in the mid-40s when Hayes hit the water around 8 a.m., and the pond was colder than that. But Hayes was surging with adrenaline and didn’t feel the chill as he dove in , trying to cover the distance as quickly as he could. He was underwater for a couple of seconds, then came up and took a few more strokes, and he was at the car.

With the vehicle tipping forward and to the left, the rear passenger door was the only one not submerged. Treading water, he pulled on the door handle, and it flew open. Scared and still struggling to get her bearings, Apollon was jolted by the sight of Hayes floating just outside her suddenly wide-open back door. “You have to get out of the car right now!” he yelled to her.
“You need to!” he urged. “You need to get to me.”

Apollon saw she’d have to crawl over the console between the seats—not easy to do in a car listing in the opposite direction, especially as her instinct was to move delicately and protect her belly. She swung her legs around so her feet were pointing toward Hayes. Now lying on her side, she pushed with her arms and slid up the console, inching toward the back seat, gravity working against her at every turn.

For centuries, lost cargo sparked fierce battles over who had the right to claim treasures washed ashore.

In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships , so huge they were referred to as “ floating cities ,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves.

The disaster quickly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage , the “right of wreck.”

It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.”

That said, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord . In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.)

Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling . Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter).
Lonely Diarist of the High Seas
As ship stewardess, Ella Sheldon tended to upper-crust women onboard and battled a range of workplace demons. Her journals tell her story.

The resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee . Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective.

In 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “ man, dog, or cat ” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat)

Legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)
“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne. “I am convinced…

“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne . “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a letter of objection from one Rosalie Levine of Lakewood, California.

“I live alone, I must control my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV dinner’s price “cannot possibly be bettered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready dinner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to prepare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up afterward.” While none of these advantages were accidental, the oft-told story of the concept’s emergence begins with a corporate crisis.

“In 1953, someone at Swanson colossally miscalculated the level of the American appetite for Thanksgiving turkey, leaving the company with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it . “Inspired by the trays of pre-prepared food served on airlines,” Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas set the machinery in motion to package the unwanted meat with gravy and sides like cornbread and sweet potatoes, ready for stocking in America’s frozen-food aisles.

The following year, Swanson sold ten million such “TV dinners,” a name attributed to both the shape of the boxes and the form of entertainment families tended to enjoy while eating the meals within. “In 1950, only 9 percent of U.S. households had television sets — but by 1955, the number had risen to more than 64 percent, and by 1960, to more than 87 percent,” writes Kovie Biakolo in a more recent Smithsonian piece . (Among the Smithsonian Institution’s holdings, incidentally, is an original Swanson TV dinner tray .) Another breakthrough came with the introduction of microwave-safe trays, bringing total preparation time under ten minutes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Americans rekindled their love affair with frozen meals, “spending nearly 50 percent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

Where holiday and commercial lore intersect, the details tend to get complicated. Swanson’s TV dinner did have its precedents: the core technology for quick-freezing packaged foods was invented over a century ago by entrepreneur Clarence Birdseye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remembers as “little cryogenic miracles”), and in the late 1940s, different companies planned or attempted to bring frozen meals to market under brands like Strato-Plates, FridgiDinners, and One-Eyed Eskimo. None of those names tapped into the technology transforming not just American mass culture, but also the American way of life. In the fifties, associations with television (and, indeed, with air travel) carried a kind of sophistication they certainly don’t have today. Perhaps Craig Claiborne would be pleased that Americans never quite accepted microwaved TV dinners as a substitute for the Thanksgiving meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is another matter entirely.

Alice’s Restaurant. It’s now a Thanksgiving classic, and something of a tradition around here. Recorded in 1967, the 18+ minute counterculture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, starting on Thanksgiving Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hippie-bating police officer, by the name of William “Obie” Obanhein , arrested Arlo for littering. (Cultural footnote: Obie previously posed for several Norman Rockwell paintings, including the well-known painting, “The Runaway,” that graced a 1958 cover of The Saturday Evening Post .) In fairly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a misdemeanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the story isn’t over. Not by a long shot.

Later, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the petty crime ironically becomes a basis for disqualifying him from military service in the Vietnam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bitterness as the song builds into a satirical protest against the war: “I’m sittin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, houses and villages after bein’ a litterbug.” And then we’re back to the cheery chorus again: “You can get anything you want, at Alice’s Restaurant.”
We have featured Guthrie’s classic during past years. But, for this Thanksgiving, we give you the illustrated version.

How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes

Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable , that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage.

Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop , the golden fan of the gingko , the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe .
In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).

But if we trouble it with light,
So love the thousand knives as they enter
and see your shape still sitting.
See that you too belong to paws
of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled
Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us.
The big secret is this: No one else can brave you.
in this world we’re pressed into,

"The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth..."
“The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth…”

“No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself . And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness , completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry ( public library ) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society .

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:

In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.
In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming , Warren adds:

The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:

How does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life.

Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change , then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit .

Revolutionary-era women spun flax as resistance against British rule and colonial gender norms.

250 years ago, as the leaves changed and the weather turned colder, General George Washington and the Continental Army marched across Pennsylvania and New Jersey. In the evenings, Washington retreated to his marquee tents, which served as both the center of field command and the general’s private quarters. Through the rain and the ice, Washington camped under a canopy made of linen—trusty, waterproof, and American-made .

In the 1760s, as taxes on British imported goods rose under King George III (r. 1760–1820), American colonists turned to homespun textiles as symbols of resistance and ultimately, independence. One of these textiles was linen , spun and woven from the fibers of the flax plant. Washington’s tent was made by a Pennsylvania upholsterer rather than in private homes, but for women, spinning bees and weaving contests became a way of participating in Revolutionary activities while navigating complex gender dynamics. While cotton is king in the history of American textiles, flax played an important role in the cultural front of the American Revolution, uniting soon-to-be Americans in industriousness and self-sufficiency.

Flax, or Linum usitatissimum , is one of the oldest continuously cultivated plants in the world , with fibers discovered in the Alps dating back to 5000 BCE . It typically grows in sandy loam and temperate climates, creating blankets of slender stalks and blue flowers in the springtime. Flaxseeds can be ground and eaten or pressed into flaxseed oil or linseed oil . The former is edible and rich in mega-3s, and the latter is used in commodities ranging from paints to linoleum (a material named after the words “linen” and “oil”). But far and away, the most common use of flax is to create the durable, breathable textile—linen.

In ancient Egypt, linen made from flax was ubiquitous , appearing in everything from mummy wrappings to everyday attire. It quickly spread to Europe and beyond. In 789, the future emperor Charlemagne decreed that all households should cultivate their own flax and produce domestic textiles at home.

By the seventeenth century, the weaving of linen was a skilled craft in Europe. Peasants would typically grow, process, and spin their own flax yarn and then bring it to a local artisan— who was usually male —to weave into cloth. As the colonial world expanded, so did the linen trade. Both the Virginia Company and the Massachusetts Bay Company had unsuccessfully encouraged settlers at Jamestown and Massachusetts to cultivate flax in the early seventeenth century , but later efforts to grow the crop in North America succeeded. Linen plants were soon growing up and down the East Coast, along with the most productive colonies in the mid-Atlantic region.

In seventeenth-century North America, women spun thread but did not weave ; weaving was considered a skilled craft that only a man could hone and monetize. However, by the mid-eighteenth century, the gender norms of linen production were changing. The economy of the thirteen colonies developed rapidly, with complex networks of trade connecting the settlers to mainland England and beyond. Despite the common misconception of early American self-sufficiency, the average colonist spent more than one-quarter of their budget on imports .

Even so, they were no strangers to taxation that caused shockwaves in the homegrown textile economy. The Wool Act of 1699 prevented colonists from exporting their wool to protect the English textile industry. Weaving became a way for daughters to contribute wealth to the household at a time when it was unseemly for them to work in the field or accept wages. As historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich writes, the development of weaving among American women was “ neither an artifact of rural poverty nor a response to frontier exigency. It was a colonial adaptation to an expanding mercantile economy .” By the 1770s, the American textile industry was developing rapidly. As such, the act of turning flax into usable textile products became part of the daily lives of women, who, as Ulrich explains, “ measured their days, not in coffee spoons, but in knots and skeins .”

Gloria Steinem was booked up. There had been luncheons and interviews scheduled for the fall; a high-profile conversation with Katie Couric at 92NY and a prominent place in The New Yorker Festival’s lineup. She left appearances unfulfilled, interviews unaired, an essay unpublished and a forthcoming book. In short: Gloria Steinem was, at 92, far from done.

That energy is palpable in that very book, her memoir An Unexpected Life , published on September 22, in which she states that she planned to live to at least 100. Although she was “older than [she] ever imagined,” mortality didn’t really cross her mind much. Any why would it, when she was also “happier than [she] ever imagined” and her calendar was bursting at the seams? Part memoir, part manifesto, part consciousness raising group, An Unexpected Life is a collection of essays in which Steinem reflects on her life, lays out her worldview and looks towards the future. And just as she was in life, on the page she radiates a matter-of-fact conviction and an unflinching clarity—the result of more than sixty years spent organizing a movement.

Her story begins long before she would become the most prominent face of second-wave feminism (although Steinem would reject this label), with a bruised childhood in Toledo, Ohio. She spent stretches of her young life on the road, until her father left when she was ten years old, leaving her in a rat-infested home caring for her increasingly mentally ill mother. With a childhood spent longing for warm kitchens and cookie cutter family units, it is striking that Steinem would grow up to spend so much of her adult life traveling around the country, more often than not living out of a suitcase. But even more formative than her earliest years, perhaps, was the time spent in India in her early 20s, an experience that would become the very foundation of her feminism.

Although mortality was far from Steinem’s mind, it is apparent in these pages that she was hyperaware of her legacy. “At my age, in this still hierarchical time, people often ask me if I’m ‘passing the torch,’” she wrote in her 1983 book Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellion s . “I explain that I’m keeping my torch, thank you very much—and I’m using it to light the torches of others.”

She is doing just that in An Unexpected Life , a text bursting with a kind of hopeful exhilaration about what could be. “Nothing is more exciting than making the invisible visible. It’s like finding the end in a ball of yarn,” she wrote. “Pull on it, and gradually the whole of patriarchy unravels.” At times, she gets as literal as bullet-point lists on how to best organize a feminist movement. There are glimmers of the—often cited—shortcomings of the women’s movement that she was at the helm of herself. “Insist on multiracial women who represent the movement,” is one such takeaway of Steinem’s. “Otherwise, people will have a distorted view.” There is an added poignancy to the essays upon her passing; a book that is as much about her life as it is a handbook for movement building. “Whatever my story might be to other people,” Steinem wrote, “I hope something has ripple effects that I myself may never see.”

One such ripple effect concerns her beloved home, an apartment in a brownstone building on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. “If time and ingenuity allow,” Steinem wrote in the book’s prologue, “I hope to acquire the other floors in this house and leave this whole building as a refuge for diverse women who need a place to stay or just to meet.”

Steinem first moved into her apartment in 1968, together with a roommate. Throughout the years, the apartment grew not only in square footage but in function. The single unit became an entire floor, which became three floors. Her living room had been a meeting place for over fifty years, where she hosted gatherings and talking circles up until this very year. She held meeting on topics ranging from women’s health to misinformation in the media—a meeting in that very living room had led to the founding of Ms. Magazine in 1971. The Radicalization of Eugene V. Debs and the Country He Radicalized in Return
On a foggy September morning in 1877, Eugene Victor Debs adjusted his suit collar and set out for the Indiana State House.

On a foggy September morning in 1877, Eugene Victor Debs adjusted his suit collar and set out for the Indiana State House. Just shy of twenty-two years old, he’d been a member of his labor union, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, for barely two and a half years. But today he would deliver the opening address to its national convention.

Horse-drawn wagons and carriages rolled through the downtown streets of Indianapolis, clacking on the cobblestones and kicking up gravel as paved stretches came to an end. Lavishly ornamented cast-iron buildings mingled with simple brick structures; steam whistles sounded from the railroad tracks bound for the teeming Union Depot, the first in the country to bring all train traffic to a central hub. City leaders were thinking longterm here. Meatpacking was the city’s other big industry, Kingan and Company’s mammoth plant one of the largest in the world, its state-of-the-art chilling system allowing year-round production in these days before refrigeration.

Indianapolis wasn’t Chicago or St. Louis, Midwestern metropolises with populations in the hundreds of thousands, but its 75,000 inhabitants painted a smaller-scale picture of a rapidly industrializing America. With all the corresponding possibilities and cruelties. The boom-and-bust of capitalism had gone bust four years before in the so-called Panic of 1873, an economic disaster nearly as severe as the Great Depression of the 1930s—and joblessness persisted in Indianapolis, as elsewhere. Workers terrified of being laid off grudgingly accepted wage cuts. Politicians responded to calls for a public jobs program with creative new punishments instead: fines for begging, a proposed workhouse “where all persons incapable of paying fines” would be forced to smash stones to pave more city streets.

Soon, Gene Debs would have seen the Indiana State House come into view. A white wooden fence edged the tree-lined lawn—the trunks like matchsticks, branches draped with green leaves holding on despite the imminent change in seasons. The dome of the state capitol rose above, a grand if crumbling structure of blue limestone and gray stuccoed columns patterned on the Greek Parthenon. Debs—amiable and outgoing, a bit over six feet tall, with a slim but solid build—entered the capitol and mounted the stairs to the House of Representatives’ chamber on the upper floor, which the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen was borrowing for the convention. He greeted his fellow delegates, who had exchanged their soot-stained work clothes for suits and ties.

Theirs was grimy, dangerous work. Firemen shoveled the coal that powered steam engines into the locomotive’s firebox, which was prone to explosion. Every month the firemen’s magazine carried grim news of widowed wives, orphaned children, maimed railroaders. Train derailments and collisions were ubiquitous. Railroad workers made up the bulk of workplace injuries in Gilded Age America: by one count 56 percent of the broken ribs, 50 percent of broken arms, 41 percent of broken legs, 71 percent of severed arms, and all of the amputated legs.

Nearly one in four trainmen could expect to die on the job if he worked for thirty years; only coal mining was as lethal. The work was well paid by the standards of the day, with veteran engineers often able to own their own home, but shifts were long and irregular, running anywhere from twelve to twenty-four hours, or longer. “It is no uncommon thing,” one railroader said, “for an engineer to go for nearly a week without sleep except in snatches on the road or waiting on a branch or engine house.” Workers lived close to the railyards, knowing that at a moment’s notice they could be gone for days or weeks. The imperatives of their employers, rather than their own individual wants or collective needs, governed workers’ lives.

Not that Debs begrudged the railroad companies. If the work was too dangerous or too demanding, the hours too long or the bosses too harsh, it was up to railroad workers to prove themselves worthy of more respect. Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science. Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology, physics, chemistry…

Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science . Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology , physics , chemistry , quantum physics , quantum computing , fungi , and many others besides. But with his latest map, Domain of Science creator Dominic Walliman has turned away from the scientific realm — or rather, he’s ventured into the larger intellectual territory out of which it emerged. His new Map of Philosophy , which he explains in the video above , includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiquity like Thales, Laozi, Confucius, and the Buddha, who lived and died before science as we know it.

That hardly means that they’ve become irrelevant today. There still exist societies described as Confucian or Buddhist, of course, but in the Western world, we’re more likely to refer back to — and, in many cases, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. “They basically laid the intellectual foundation of Western philosophy, science, and political thought,” says Walliman. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unexamined life is not worth living, which “hits pretty hard in the age of the distraction economy.”)

Though often mentioned together, these three ancient Greeks occupy slightly different positions on the philosophical map, with Socrates closer to the land of ethics, Plato to metaphysics, and Aristotle to epistemology.

As Walliman explains, “epistemology studies knowledge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it differs from faith or opinions,” while also seeking out its limits. Aristotle’s rigor in testing and organizing knowledge makes him, in a sense, one of the earliest scientists. Though his body of theory may no longer be our best means of understanding how the world works, his systematic pursuit of such an understanding set him apart from much of the ancient intellectual world. The islands off the coast of the map’s mainland represent subfields still actively explored today, like the philosophies of mind, language, politics, religion, and science — which, for all its prestige, remains as subject to philosophical inquiry as any other area of human endeavor. The map of philosophy shows us not a rarefied, mostly abandoned territory, but the place where we all live our lives, examined or otherwise.

Fingers, frozen to the bone in the damp cold, barely obey.

A trembling hand fumbles in the scratchy wool of an overcoat pocket for another five-round clip. That damned bolt again. The last round stuck fast. One strike. Another—with a numb palm. New clip…stiff bolt handle forward and down…chamber a new round and close the breech.
So cold. Eyes ache from peering into the fogged dark. The head throbs from gunfire crackling since morning.
A minor railway stop, Kruty, lost in bleak fields, near a nameless hamlet beyond Nizhyn.

“They’re coming, still coming, stay alert!” officers shout hoarsely from the snow-covered embankment, voices strained. Through icy fog and under the dim light of a veiled moon, shadows advance across the wide field, cut through by endless rails.
The Reds send another wave into the attack.
A flash splits the darkness on the far horizon. Then a boom, and an explosion close by. The blasts throb like a pulse in the temples.
Teeth clench. The head pulls inward, wishing never to hear and see, shrapnel whistles overhead. This time for sure.
A hoarse shout—the machine guns burst to life, tearing the darkness with short volleys, chewing through belts of cartridges.
Around, thin lines of defense stretch across the silvery ribbon of rails: a motley battalion of whoever God sent, in whatever they had, with God knows-what instead of proper weapons.

Students from Kyiv. Young cadets in old overcoats, in felt boots, with grimy yellow-blue armbands on their sleeves. Gymnasium students, mere schoolboys who had hardly ever fired a shot before, in ordinary clothes, standing off to the left to keep away from harm. Fiery, dreamy lads who did not run, too ashamed to turn their backs.
So this was the revolution, marching from Petrograd, for the people’s happiness, of course. Cutting down the “old world” in its path, reeking of strong liquor.

One student—his face still untouched by a razor—keeps nervously adjusting his round spectacles again and again, brushing frost-dust with trembling fingers. They had all volunteered. Shivering in the cold, breathing heavily. Clumsily digging shallow trenches. They weren’t meant to be here. Schoolboys, maybe good enough to haul ammo, nothing more. So they were sent to a “relatively quiet sector” of the front, but ended up encountering the main enemy forces.

A handful of junior officers, none over thirty, stand beside them in Russian army uniforms, their epaulets torn off, imperial cockades missing. This was the young army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic—its most devoted part.
“Matviy, keep an eye on the youngsters here!” A gloved hand claps his shoulder, and the officer ducks low, moving on to steady the thin line.

Another deep, dull thud, one that rings sharp in the skull, not just the ears. The soft stubble of a cheek touches the frozen wooden stock again. Lungs pull in frost. Another shot into the darkness merges into the deafening cannonade. And another. And again.

They keep coming with bayonets fixed, advancing toward the machine guns across the field to the station. Navy peacoats, quilted jackets, caps, red armbands. They’ve been coming since morning. Sailors of the Baltic Fleet. Red Guards from Petrograd and Moscow…no strangers to this kind of work.
There they lie, bastards. Dozens of black mounds, sprawled in the dark after a day of relentless charges—frozen mid-agony, a bullet still in the gut.
The Reds are advancing on Kyiv.
So this was the revolution, marching from Petrograd, for the people’s happiness, of course. Cutting down the “old world” in its path, reeking of strong liquor.
Kharkiv is lost, Poltava is lost, Chernihiv is lost. Through forests and steppe, along rails from Russia, the armored trains grind toward the Ukrainian capital.
Another heavy blow from the Bolshevik battery—and now they’re pulling him away: sotnyk Omelchenko, the student company leader, his head torn open by shrapnel, blood gushing from beneath his cap.
You won’t make it to Kyiv, friend. Remember us up there.
We can’t hold this alone. Not for long.
Finding My Way in the Wilderness with Brush and Pen

In 1994, as a refugee from New York City advertising (an accidental career resulting from a failed attempt to convert my biology degree into artistic fame in the big city), I returned to my home state of Vermont and dove headlong into wildlife art, crisscrossing the U.S. for six years on the national art show circuit. I didn’t write anything but birthday cards to my daughters.

Right in the middle of a show out west in the winter of 2000/2001, it hit me: I’d become as much a teamster as an artist, and I felt cut off from what inspired me to paint. I ditched my late summer schedule and planned an August/September, 330-mile “source-to-salt” canoe trip on the Missinaibi River, which flows north to James Bay (I bought my first canoe with my paper route money when I was 11). The trip wasn’t to be an escapist adventure, but work: a painting trip and a chance to reconnect with my Muse, as a classicist would say.

It also introduced writing into my creative repertoire. Realizing that hardly anyone would notice if I disappeared into the wilderness for a month, I contacted an art magazine that liked the artist-on-a-canoe-trip angle, and a canoeing magazine that liked the canoeist-on-an-art-trip angle. I wasn’t sure what I would write, but I figured something would come to mind on the river.

I’d assumed I’d have to go alone with an artist’s itinerary, but at an art show opening in June, John Pitcher, a pre-eminent U.S. wildlife artist, asked to join me. On the river, John and I became fast friends and discussed future trips, but in Mattice, Ontario, after 130 miles, he had to return, and I continued solo.

As soon as Mattice disappeared behind a bend, the enormity of what I was doing settled in. I was alone, facing 200 miles of wild river through roadless wilderness. On the one hand, I was keenly aware that without anyone to help, even a minor mishap could cascade into tragedy. On the other, the river held my undivided attention.
The wild expanses I have experienced aren’t alien places, but reminders that the wild is where we all come from.

That first night alone, I camped at the Kettle Falls portage, and in a substantial blow to my self-image as an adventurer, I was hit with an acute attack of loneliness. I focused on setting camp and starting dinner, but I couldn’t shake the intense melancholy. Then the westering sun lit the river’s east bank with an evening glow. Hoping for another distraction, I set to painting while my dinner boiled. I had to work fast to catch the light, but before long (and to my pleasant surprise), the painting started to come alive. A surge of euphoria welled up out of nowhere and washed the loneliness away in a tidal wave so intense that, for a few moments, I wondered if I was OK. The weirdest part was a heartwarming sense of connection, not just to my surroundings, but to people—not anyone in particular, but everyone. I was never lonely on the river again.

That evening, as I dutifully recorded the day’s events in the journal the magazines had asked me to keep, I discovered that my new assignment was more than just a travelogue. The small painting that had precipitated one of the most intense emotional reactions of my life could, ironically, do nothing to describe or explain the internal transformation I’d undergone. But writing could.
The Way North – Kettle Falls, Missinaibi River . Acrylic field painting, September 4, 2001.

Over the next week, I made friends with Canada Jays and sandpipers, talked to rocks and various pieces of my gear, all of whom were generally supportive. On the other hand, an oblivious bull moose nearly killed me by accident, and a large bear looked like he was contemplating doing it on purpose.

But the river and forest offered only indifference. There was sound: birds, wind, the current along my hull or surging through rapids, but no noise and nothing I did seemed to matter. The ageless enormity of the planet pressed in, a wild Earth utterly unconcerned with humans, and as I thought back on the dizzying diversity of life that “Mother Earth” has birthed, provided for, and let pass away through the eons, I realized she is an impassive parent.
