One of the most important things I have learned about life is that joy is a choice, an orientation, a practice of bending the mind in the direction of gladness — a choice increasingly countercultural in our age of competitive complaint, and yet all the more urgent precisely because our world gives us so many valid reasons for despair. “Experience of conflict and a load of suffering has taught me that what matters above all is to celebrate joy… Life is wasted when we make it more terrifying, precisely because it is so easy to do so,” the artist René Magritte wrote in his timeless manifesto for the courage of joy in the wake of the second World War of his life. “We’ve all had too much sorrow — now is the time for joy,” Nick Cave sang an epoch later as he contemplated the paradox of joy against the backdrop of unimaginable loss.

Joy is not difficult to find, but it can be difficult to trust — partly because the merchants of pseudo-morality have sold us the dangerous myth that, in an unjust world, despair is an emblem of our solidarity with justice, and partly because in this age of grandiosity, we have forgotten that joy is a plurality of smallnesses: a function of what Hermann Hesse called “the little joys” that light up a life with presence.

We need them, these reminders that joy is not a denial of suffering but the fulcrum of our resilience in its midst; that it comes to us not with horns and cymbals but as a distant whisper from the birthplace of the ordinary, not like a bouquet of roses offered with champagne but like the lovely little weed blooming through a crack in the sidewalk of the quotidian. And that is precisely what artist-philosopher Maira Kalman offers in her book Joy ( public library ) — a love letter to the sweet strangeness of life, to its unboastful wonderland of small miracles, to the way it expands and expands and expands the moment we contract the aperture of attention onto a single unit of gladness.
It begins where we must begin:

And then it goes where we, short-termists of the present, rarely go: into the lives of some of her heroes who lived through times and turmoils far more unimaginable than ours: She paints Alfred Dreyfus sitting in his prison cell on Devil’s Island; she paints the bedroom in which Beethoven, fully deaf, wrote “Ode to Joy” ; she paints Virginia Woolf and her “surprisingly colorful” sitting room just before she filled her coat pockets with stones and waded into the River Ouse; she paints Kafka under the black hat he wore as a helmet of despair, his hand rested tenderly on his beloved dog.

As if to remind us that we are always in relationship with those whose lives have touched ours, whether living or dead, whether or not we have ever met them, she paints her imaginary conversations with Gertrude Stein, with James Baldwin, with Vladimir Nabokov.

Dog punctuate this love letter to joy, cradled in arms and curled in corners, peeking from the pages with their searching eyes and their uncomplicated sweetness: “Isn’t that the answer to everything,” she writes with an eye to a friend who tends to her four dogs “with unlimited care and love.”
And people, of course, so many people with their strange and soulful faces, each a universe of feeling conjured up with just a few brush strokes.

She reverences trees, “kind and strong and loving,” and a medieval painting of “a saint with a terrific hairdo” at the Met, and a beautiful man with a porkpie hat at the bookstore, and the fig tree in a friend’s backyard, and people singing, and a young man playing Bach on his violin under the cherry tree, and Pablo Casals playing Bach on his cello while smoking a pipe.
Do children not give us our reason?

Between Psyche and Cyborg: Carl Jung’s Legacy and the Countercultural Courage to Reclaim the Deeply Human in…
"A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent."
“A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent.”

“To be a human being among people and to remain one forever, no matter in what circumstances… that’s what life is all about, that’s its task,” the young Dostoyevsky exulted in a letter to his brother just after his death sentence was repealed — death, that great clarifying force for what it means to be alive, what the stakes and sanctities of living are.

In the two centuries since, our understanding of what it means to be human, to be mortal and imperfect and ablaze with feeling, has altered dramatically as we have entrusted the cold logic of computation with answering the soul’s cry for connection, for creativity, for meaning — something Dostoyevsky’s contemporary Samuel Butler anticipated in his far-seeing admonition against the dehumanization of humanity in the hands of our machines , something that has metastasized in today’s technocratic cult of posthumanism.

In Jung vs Borg: Finding the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age , Glen Slater bridges ecology, depth psychology, systems theory, and various post-Cartesian philosophies to explore how this civilizational cult has effected “a widening divide between fabrication and authenticity, a loss of more self-aware and soulful modes of living, and an increase in anxiety and depression,” and what we can do to rewild the psyche and reclaim the soul.

He begins by drawing an analogy between the catalytic impact of Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring on awakening the modern ecological conscience and the need for a conscious awakening from the dangerous dream of posthumanism into which Silicon Valley has lulled us. Just as the industrial capitalism of Carson’s era commodified our planet’s ecosystems and elemental resources, Slater observes that digital capitalism has “turned our habits of mind into the earth’s most valuable commodity”; just as Carson pioneered the holistic view of ecology that may be our only path to saving Earth, her contemporary Carl Jung pioneered the holistic view of psychology that might, just might, save the human soul from death by commodification.
Whether or not we have turned the ecological corner, there is more consciousness about the way we relate to the world around us and the actions required to avert a climate catastrophe.

However, the world within us, the inner life of thought and emotion, is another matter. Here integrative understanding has been resisted. The human psyche, the ecosystem of the mind, with its own structures and dynamics, our relation to which is surely as significant as our relation to the outer world, now faces its own significant disruption, one that essentially parallels the syndrome Carson described… The depths of human nature are becoming harder to recognize and protect. Abundant information has furthered scientific knowledge but not human understanding. It has instead left us dazed, confused, and disoriented. Attention, motivation, identity, self-image, and the capacity to reason clearly and imagine deeply are all impacted… While the advantages of digital technologies are impressed upon us at every turn, the rapid entry of these technologies into every aspect of life is evidently impacting our ecology of mind.
With an eye to the urgency of “moving beyond objectification of the earth and of the bodies and minds that inhabit it,” he adds:

The technosphere now overlays the ecosphere and we cannot help but inhale its post-industrial gases. Virtuality has begun to displace reality, making the ground of human existence hard to discern… The human psyche and the nature of the whole person are not only suffering in this technospheric environment, the suffering has itself been given over to technological solutions, resulting in a vicious cycle.

The penchant for digital ways of relating, expanding faith in AI, and the one-sided education designed to service these things are combining to generate reductive conceptions of psychological life. Necessary Losses: The Life-Shaping Art of Letting Go
"We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss. And we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and…

“The art of losing isn’t hard to master,” Elizabeth Bishop wrote in one of the great masterpieces of poetry . “Every mortal loss is an Immortal Gain,” William Blake wrote two centuries before her in his beautiful letter to a bereaved father .

We dream of immortality because we are creatures made of loss — the death of the individual is what ensured the survival of the species along the evolutionary vector of adaptation — and made for loss: All of our creativity, all of our compulsive productivity, all of our poems and our space telescopes, are but a coping mechanism for our mortality, for the elemental knowledge that we will lose everything and everyone we cherish as we inevitably return our borrowed stardust to the universe.

And yet the measure of life, the meaning of it, may be precisely what we make of our losses — how we turn the dust of disappointment and dissolution into clay for creation and self-creation, how we make of loss a reason to love more fully and live more deeply.

That is what Judith Viorst explores in her 1987 consolation of a book Necessary Losses ( public library ) — an inquiry into the profound and far-reaching relationship between our losses and our gains, revealing renunciation as a fulcrum of growth. She paints the vast landscape of loss upon which life plays out:

When we think of loss we think of the loss, through death, of people we love. But loss is a far more encompassing theme in our life. For we lose not only through death, but also by leaving and being left, by changing and letting go and moving on. And our losses include not only our separations and departures from those we love, but our conscious and unconscious losses of romantic dreams, impossible expectations, illusions of freedom and power, illusions of safety — and the loss of our own younger self, the self that thought it always would be unwrinkled and invulnerable and immortal.

These necessary losses… we confront when we are confronted by the inescapable fact… that we are essentially out here on our own; that we will have to accept — in other people and ourselves — the mingling of love with hate, of the good with the bad;… that there are flaws in every human connection; that our status on this planet is implacably impermanent; and that we are utterly powerless to offer ourselves or those we love protection — protection from danger and pain, from the in-roads of time, from the coming of age, from the coming of death; protection from our necessary losses.
These losses are a part of life — universal, unavoidable, inexorable. And these losses are necessary because we grow by losing and leaving and letting go.

As a sculpture is shaped by what is chiseled off from the block of stone, so too are we shaped by what we lose — by choice, with all the complexities and difficulties of letting go, or by the scythe of chance, which takes away as impartially as it gives. Viorst writes:

The road to human development is paved with renunciation. Throughout our life we grow by giving up. We give up some of our deepest attachments to others. We give up certain cherished parts of ourselves. We must confront, in the dreams we dream, as well as in our intimate relationships, all that we never will have and never will be. Passionate investment leaves us vulnerable to loss. And sometimes, no matter how clever we are, we must lose… It is only through our losses that we become fully developed human beings.

We enter the realm of loss the moment the umbilical cord is cut to sever what Viorst calls the “blurred-boundary bliss of mother-child oneness” — the primal loss that sets off the ongoing task of becoming ourselves . From this origin point, she traces the lifelong vector of losses and gains:

Exchanging the illusion of absolute shelter and absolute safety for the triumphant anxieties of standing alone… we become a moral, responsible, adult self, discovering — within the limitations imposed by necessity — our freedoms and choices. And in giving up our impossible expectations, we become a lovingly connected self, renouncing ideal visions of perfect friendship, marriage, children, family life for the sweet imperfections of all-too-human relationships. While the term ‘Friendsgiving’ is new, the tradition has been around for decades – found family and…
A food studies scholar provides some tips for throwing the perfect Friendsgiving gathering.

One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.
While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.
If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.

Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity.

Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.

The Language of Gender Diversity in Zulu
Once used to stigmatize queer people, traditional Zulu terms are being reclaimed as expressions of identity.

South Africa’s constitution enshrines the rights of LGBTQIA+ people. And yet discrimination and violence toward queer and gender nonconforming people are widespread in that country. In Zulu communities, which are concentrated in the province of KwaZulu-Natal, many people view these identities as something foreign to their traditional culture. And the Zulu terms used to describe them, such as isitabane (plural izitabane), are widely considered offensive.

But Zulu gender and sexuality researchers Sizwesamajobe G. Sithole and Lindiwe Khuzwayo use those words to describe themselves. Working with anthropologist Maheshvari Naidu, they argue that using Indigenous terms can help situate queer identities within a decolonial framework.

Sithole, Khuzwayo, and Naidu set out to help reclaim Zulu words for queer and gender-diverse people, as well as spiritual aspects of those identities. They write that their interest in the topic stemmed partly from violent statements made by a former radio personality, Ngizwe Mchunu, who objected to izitabane marrying in traditional Zulu attire.

In fact, they write, it was colonial governments and Christianization that brought the widespread frameworks of anti-sodomy laws and the concept of sexual sin to African societies. Without arguing that it’s possible to go back to a precolonial worldview , they suggest looking at Zulu tradition for different ways of approaching sex and gender.
Sex between people of the same gender has existed for millennia. But anthropologists in sub-Saharan Africa often ignored or distorted those relationships.

In traditional Zulu spiritual practices, for example, men may be referred to as Gogo (grandmother) and women as mkhulu (grandfather), reflecting the embodiment of ancestors and spiritual power regardless of biological sex. And in one Zulu creation story, human beings originated in a cave, and the first person to come out of the cave was “ncukubili,” a term used for intersex people, and specifically for a person with both male and female genital organs.

Like izitabane and ncukubili, other terms related to gender and sexual differences are often used in insulting ways. This includes “ungquingili,” a term that suggests disability based on being born with atypical sex characteristics, and “inkonkoni,” the name of a species of wildebeest known to engage in male-male sex acts.

Yet some queer and transgender people the authors worked with saw themselves in these terms. One trans man referred to himself as an “Inkonkoni,” saying that someone unfamiliar with wildebeests may mistake one for a cow, but “the moment they see a real wildebeest, they will realize that it is a wild animal.” He used this analogy to describe his experience being visibly out of place in girls’ spaces as a child.

While other LGBTQIA+ people may find such terms painful to use, Sithole, Khuzwayo, and Naidu argue that they can help situate such identities in decolonial terms that focus less on individual autonomy and more on relationships among living people, ancestors, land, and the more-than-human world.
“The appropriation of these gender terms moves power from the perpetrators who use these names to shame and dehumanize izitabane,” they write.
When Jorge Luis Borges Co-Wrote a Surreal Sci-Fi Noir Film: Invasión (1969)
“La ciudad es más que la gente.” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not…

“ La ciudad es más que la gente. ” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión , the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when Invasión came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as Jorge Luis Borges — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Another major contributor to Invasión ’s screenplay was Borges’ longtime friend, occasional collaborator, and junior colleague in letters Adolfo Bioy Casares . Anyone who’s read about their relationship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of published diaries, simply titled Borges ) knows how deeply entangled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And anyone who knows Buenos Aires will recognize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echoing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ classical inspiration for this project, which transposes the city under siege of Homer’s Troy into mid-century Latin America, where a small group of resistance members organize against an arriving army of menacing white-coated invaders.

Though Borges wasn’t exactly one for topicality in his own ficciones , it wouldn’t be wholly unreasonable to make an allegorical reading of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argentina was ruled by Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, one of several dictators in the country’s twentieth-century history. It came out during the dictatorship of Juan Carlos Onganía Carballo. And the 1976 military coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in power banished it to an official non-existence, seen only in the most underground screenings. It wasn’t until the nineteen-nineties that Invasión was rediscovered and made whole out of partial prints found in France, the country to which Santiago had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in one version with optional English and French subtitles, and another, higher resolution version with French subtitles only.

Viewers today may be quick to notice the obvious budgetary limitations, manifest in odd-sounding foley work and theatrical death scenes, but the cinematic vitality of its mixture of film noir, Nouvelle Vague , political thriller, and even science fiction remains undeniable. (With the chases and explosions it manages, it may even partially qualify as an action movie.) So does the atmosphere of the real locations — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the climactic football stadium — that constitute its alternately stately and desolate setting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a character, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many other questions about Invasión , there is no one answer.

Given recent history, the prospect of hundreds of young men meeting on Facebook, then traveling from around the country to a central U.S. location might sound like reasonable cause for alarm. Yet a convention fitting that description had nothing to do with political violence but, rather, a celebration and appreciation of the name “Josh” (full disclosure: this writer did not attend). The gathering of the Joshes in April 2021 in Nebraska could not have been more peaceful, including its finishing battle royale, conducted with pool noodles.

The Joshes had no concern for proper pool-noodle-wielding technique, if there is such a thing. But groups of people who gather around the country to stage medieval-style battles in live-action role playing (LARP) games with weapons both real and fake might benefit from pointers.

So, too, might those who choreograph sword fights on stage and screen. Where can serious historical re-creators learn how to wield a real blade in historically accurate combat? One resource can be found at Wiktenauer , a wiki devoted to collecting “all of the primary and secondary source literature that makes up the text of historical European Martial arts (HEMA) research.”

The Fior di Battaglia (“Flower of Battle”) —an Italian fencing manual by Fiore de’i Liberi dating from circa 1404—offers richly- and copiously-illustrated demonstrations of medieval Italian longsword fighting techniques. In the original manuscript, seen here and at The Getty , “the illustrations are inked sketches with gold leafing on the crowns and garters,” notes the Wiktenauer entry. They dominate the text, which “takes the form of descriptive paragraphs set in poor Italian verse, which are nevertheless fairly clear and informative.” So clear, indeed, the brooding young men of Akademia Szermierzy—a Polish group that recreates medieval sword-fighting techniques—can more than convincingly mimic the moves in the video at the top.

Once they get going, after some requisite pre-fight rigmarole, it’s impressive stuff, maybe already familiar to modern fencers and certain members of the Society for Creative Anachronism , the LARP-ing organization of amateurs recreating everything from the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. But for those who think all live-action role-playing is the equivalent of the Battle of the Joshes (or off-brand Nazis running through the streets in homemade armor), the sheer ballet of historical sword-fighting may come as a surprise — and maybe inspire a few more people to pull on the doublet and hose. In the late nineteenth century, rival breweries slashed prices in a ruthless fight to dominate America's booming beer industry.

Since wet grains ferment naturally in the presence of airborne yeasts, various forms of beer were likely discovered by multiple agriculturalists across the early farming regions of the world. The earliest archeological evidence of fermentation dates back 13,000 years . For thousands of years, beer was an artisanal product made at home, one that was sometimes safer to drink than the local water. Then the Industrial Revolution transformed beer into a mass-produced beverage.

German immigrants were largely responsible for bringing beer culture to the US. Anheuser-Busch, Pabst, Schlitz, Coors, and Yuengling, for instance, were all founded by German Americans. These giants of the industry today ( minus Schlitz ) emerged victorious from the wild and foamy “beer wars” of the late nineteenth century.
Historian Braden Neihart explores that ferocious competition in a case study of Rock Island, Illinois.

“Brewers fought constantly for market share on multiple fronts, through price dropping and undercutting each other with little concern for the immediate fallout. The end goal was survival, and the casualties along the way were the cost of sustaining business.”

In 1886, Rock Island’s three major local breweries produced a total of 80,000 barrels of beer. This was enough, Neihart figures, for an astonishing 800 beers per resident annually. Because this was well-above-average, the brewers were clearly finding additional markets in nearby towns like Moline as well as in Bettendorf and Davenport across the Mississippi in Iowa.

“Brewers operated within a fiercely capitalist market, restrained by few rules and characterized by high risk,” writes Neihart, noting that the competition was both homegrown and from big beer cities like Peoria, Chicago, and Milwaukee.

Locally, the Rock Island Brewing Company (RIBC) ended up buying its competitors, Atlantic Brewery, City Brewery, Rock Island Brewery, and Junge’s Bottling Works, by 1894. But then, in early 1895, Milwaukee-based Schlitz Brewing Company started rolling its barrels into town. On the road to becoming the nation’s largest beer producer, Schlitz dropped the price of its barrels from $6 to $4. The RIBC was forced to follow suit, though the price was ruinous for the company. The RIBC counterattacked with an advertising campaign to “Sustain Home Industry” and support local unions, which helped it weather the onslaught.
“Brewed with Blood”: The Coors Beercott of the 1970s
An unusual coalition transformed a labor dispute into one of the longest-running consumer protests in US history.

Drinkers, on the other hand, celebrated; in one locally notorious case, a construction worker’s rented room collapsed from all the hoarded cheap beer he was storing against an inevitable price increase.

Another strategy was to challenge a competitor’s ingredients and hence impugn their purity. German immigrant brewers came with the tradition of the centuries-old Reinheitsgebot “purity order.” This stated that “beer” was to be made from water, barley, and hops. As a form of time-honored branding, this meant that if you added anything else, you could be called out for faking it.

Challenging the purity of ingredients still goes on, as Neihart notes. Anheuser-Busch spent $30 million during the 2019 Super Bowl boasting that its Bud Light was made from rice while Molson Coors’ products, Miller Lite and Coors Lite, were made from corn syrup. Molson Coors subsequently took Anheuser-Busch to court. The Court of Appeals , which hopefully didn’t have to do a taste test, said the companies were free to list each other’s ingredients.

But back to the turn-of-the-twentieth-century strife and competition. It all came to a sudden end with the onset of Prohibition in January 1920. The Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution prohibited the “manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors.” The law crippled America’s robust beer industry and culture. Local brewers like the RIBC were driven out of business, but large factory producers had the wherewithal to pivot to legal “near-beers” and “soft drinks.”
Mogging is the word of the year – but men have been doing it since Shakespearean times
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.
The Collins English Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year.

The Collins website says that the word originated with the acronym AMOG – or “alpha male of the group” – which is often associated with bodybuilding forums and, more recently, the toxic culture of incels and the manosphere . But mogging has now entered mainstream language with its meaning slightly repurposed: to describe someone who is outperforming, outshining or upstaging someone.

While the verb is often used in reference to physical looks, it can also be applied in other contexts. Alex Beecroft , managing director of Collins, explained that the selection of mogging demonstrates how “each generation leaves its mark on language”, with the term seeing a 210% increase in usage in 2026.
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.

The Oxford English Dictionary contains four historic meanings of the base verb “mog”. The earliest meaning and usage comes as early as 1674, referring to card games “to exchange a card with the dealer”. A later usage means “to move on, depart, decamp”. By the mid-1800s, two new possible meanings emerged : “to walk slowly but steadily” and “to shift (a person, animal etc.) to cause to move on (esp. quickly)”.

What unites these historic meanings is the connection to movement or performance. For many men in the early modern period, the demonstration of superiority through action and movement was a key method to showcase, or perhaps fittingly, “mog” others.

New research by theatre historian Eleanor Rycroft explores this link between movement, gender and social power. Rycroft examines theatrical works by playwrights such as Shakespeare and Ben Jonson alongside historical conduct books and household management guides, revealing just how much cultural capital was attached to a man’s posture and stride.

How-to guides and etiquette books from the time told men and women how to behave, labelling certain traits as respectable and others as improper. In the 1566 English translation of Ortensio Landi’s Delectable Demaundes and Pleasaunt Questions (1566), readers were shown how to outdo other men in wit and conduct. Yet in doing so, the text also exposed the cracks in this ideal, revealing how precarious that masculine status truly was.

In his influential Book of the Courtier (1528), courtier and diplomat Baldassare Castiglione defined this quality as a “certain nonchalance, which shall conceal design and show that what is done and said is done without effort and almost without thought”.
Sprezzatura in Shakespeare and asserting manhood
Castiglione was first translated into English by Sir Thomas Hoby in 1561, and the concept of sprezzatura heavily influenced early modern English culture.

In many early modern plays, characters demonstrate the importance of asserting a mastery of manhood and, with it, upstaging others. While Shakespeare does not use the terms sprezzatura or mogging in any of his works, many men attempt to outperform or outshine other characters to assert or affirm their manly status.

In Much Ado About Nothing (first performed 1598), the “merry war” between protagonists Beatrice and Benedick – a rapid-fire exchange loaded with insults as the two characters shield their true feelings for one another – is often a source of audience amusement and laughter. However, this “skirmish of wit” points to the different expectations on men and women for Benedick across the play text: to match and ideally best Beatrice’s skill in wordplay so as not to emasculate himself.

Beatrice seems to be aware of these dynamics of masculinity, noting that Benedick “gets nothing” from their verbal exchanges – after their last encounter, “four of his five wits went halting off, and now is the whole man governed with one”. These scenes of verbal sparring might be understood as a trial of masculinity, testing Benedick’s skills in rhetoric and wordplay.

A more direct trial is captured in the penultimate scene of Shakespeare’s Henry IV Part 1 (first performed in 1597), which depicts the showdown between Prince Hal, who will eventually ascend to be Henry…
East Germany exiled singer Wolf Biermann. They only made his message louder
Fifty years ago the GDR withdrew the citizenship of the prominent leftwing dissident. It turned him into an international symbol – and cemented his place in history

November 16 marks 50 years since one of the most notorious examples of artistic censorship from the 20th century: the East German government’s stripping the citizenship of dissident singer-songwriter Wolf Biermann .
Far from quashing Biermann’s voice, this act of political exile amplified it, and cemented his place in history, underscored by a new documentary about his life story.

It is a lesson others should have done more to heed. Earlier this year, US billionaire Robert Kraft and other stadium owners banned Macklemore from their venues over pro-Palestinian remarks the singer made during his support slot on Ed Sheeran’s tour.
But in trying to silence the rapper, Kraft and his cohort unintentionally amplified his message .
The story of Biermann can tell us much about how attempts to quash the political expression of musicians have spectacularly backfired.
From East German darling to dissident
Biermann, born in 1936, became a prominent figure within East German left-wing dissident artists and intellectuals in the late 1960s. But he wasn’t always an outsider.

As the West German immigrant son of a Jewish communist killed in Auschwitz, and a mentee of Bertolt Brecht, Biermann was initially the darling of the East German press, and held a candidate membership of the Socialist Unity Party (SED).

When his lyrics became critical of the SED, however, the Stasi (secret police) began a campaign of harassment that escalated over more than a decade. It included performance bans, sabotage, intimidation, round-the-clock surveillance, bugging, reports from more than 200 Stasi informants , and even a veiled death threat.
Yet this persecution amplified Biermann’s voice and gave him an international platform.
The making of an international symbol
Western governments adopted Biermann as a potent symbol in the cultural Cold War. He acquired famous fans, including Joan Baez and Allen Ginsberg.
Numerous organisations awarded him prizes. CBS gave him a record deal, and West Berlin radio stations frequently broadcast his music into East Germany.

These broadcasts made some remarkable converts. Gerulf Pannach, a young songwriter and then Stasi informant , first heard Biermann’s music while working as a border guard. He befriended the singer, renounced the Stasi and began writing his own critical lyrics.
Pannach convinced Christian Kunert, the keyboardist of the beloved rock band Renft , to take an anti-state position in 1974.

Kunert, in turn, introduced writer and social psychologist Jürgen Fuchs – who would go on to become a prominent East German dissident – to Pannach and Biermann. He also converted his Renft band mate Thomas “Monster” Schoppe to the cause.
Closer to home, Biermann’s former stepdaughter, young rock singer and future queen of punk Nina Hagen , introduced her bandmates to Biermann.

Biermann’s inner circle was, for a time, paradoxically protected by their fame as dissidents. Aided by Western media, they flouted state controls in ways average East Germans wouldn’t dare. While the state maintained tight surveillance of Biermann’s circle, they seemed hesitant to arrest them.
But those more loosely associated with Biermann often found themselves caught in the crossfire of multiple Stasi operations to harass and crush dissidents.
This included band members of Renft, who helped Pannach bypass his performance ban and perform Biermann’s songs, and publicly denounced East German border policy.
As a result, members of Renft were repeatedly summoned and questioned by the authorities. Then the band was banned. In September 1975, a local licensing board told Renft they “no longer exist”.
Taboo themes in Pannach’s lyrics were the pretext for the ban , but declassified Stasi documents suggest the state ultimately targeted them as proxies for Biermann.
The regime accidentally elevated a popular East German rock band to anti-state legends.

A further attempt to neutralise Renft through conscription and a tax investigation converted the band’s thus far apolitical founder, Klaus Jentzsch, into a gifted anti-state organiser. With Biermann’s help, he coordinated a transnational multi-media campaign.

Meteorites fascinated ancient Egyptians—just look at King Tut’s ‘space dagger’
Meteoric iron was revered across the ancient Mediterranean.

In August 2026, an analysis of iron from ancient Greek tombs revealed surprising results . The objects surveyed included weapons and jewelry from around 3,000 to 4,000 years ago. Most of them were fashioned from regular old iron ore, but around 10 rings were made of iron from outer space—aka from meteorites that crash-landed on Earth.

It seems that, among the upper classes of Bronze Age Greece, rings fashioned from this out-of-this-world metal were all the rage. Before people learned how to extract iron from ore by melting it at super-high temperatures—a process called smelting—the only source of metallic iron was the occasional space rock . This material, known as meteoric iron , is rare worldwide, but especially in Greece, where approaching meteors usually disappear into the sea rather than make landfall.
Researchers believe that the Greek meteoric rings were actually imported from Egypt: a land with a special relationship to this metal from the skies.
Egyptians had meteoric iron early, but smelted iron came late

Meteoric iron can be identified because it’s purer than the iron ore that naturally occurs on Earth, with a higher proportion of nickel mixed into it. Because meteoric iron “already arrives on Earth in metallic form,” says Victoria Almansa-Villatoro, a professor of Egyptology at Yale University, “it’s very malleable” and can be shaped more easily than unrefined ore.

The Egyptians started working with this rare material early. “The oldest meteoric iron objects in the world come from Egypt,” says Almansa-Villatoro: Nine small beads , excavated from a site called Gerzeh along the bank of the Nile about 20 miles south of Cairo, are the oldest artifacts discovered made from space rocks. They are dated to around 3,200 BCE, more than a thousand years older than the 10 meteoric iron rings found in Greece.

Not only are the Gerzeh beads older than any other meteoric iron objects, they are much, much older than widespread iron smelting in Egypt. Almansa-Villatoro explains that “Egypt was relatively late in comparison with other Near Eastern civilizations to start smelting iron.” By the time the Egyptians were producing iron on a large scale in the 500s BCE, ancient people in Anatolia and other regions had been doing it for about five hundred years.

A major reason for this late adoption was Egypt’s natural resources. Iron smelting forges burned a lot of wood charcoal, and Egypt had no large forests. For centuries, the Egyptians relied on bronze, which cost less fuel to produce. It wasn’t until major changes in political and trade networks, including pressure to match the iron arsenals of foreign enemies like the Assyrians , that the Egyptians finally made the shift .

While early iron weapons and armor were not automatically better than bronze ones, iron proved easier to repair, and could be strengthened through further reworking. But objects like the Gerzeh beads show that the ancient Egyptians shaped small amounts of meteoric iron long before they knew how to extract it from ore.
King Tut’s “space dagger” and other ancient objects made from meteorites

The Gerzeh iron beads were incorporated into jewelry with gems and gold, hinting at their perceived value. All of the other Egyptian objects believed to be made of meteoric iron are similarly small and mostly decorative. The largest and most spectacular is a dagger with a meteoric iron blade more than eight inches long . It was found in the tomb of Egypt’s famous pharaoh, Tutankhamun, who died around 1,323 BCE.

Government records from the reign of Tutankhamun’s grandfather, Amenhotep III, mention an Anatolian king gifting a dagger to the Pharaoh. “People have speculated that this was the same dagger,” says Almansa-Villatoro. “Because, why would they make such a big deal about this king receiving a dagger from a foreign leader, unless it’s made of a very important or very rare material?” As seen with the recent findings from Greece, demand for meteoric iron in the ancient Mediterranean was international.

World’s fastest animal may gain habitat by 2080
But that doesn’t automatically mean its population will grow.

While climate change represents a threat to most animal populations, the reality isn’t quite as straight forward. As the landscape reacts to a shifting climate, some species might actually see their habitat expand.

That could be the case for peregrine falcons ( Falco peregrinus ), the fastest animal on the planet, living in the United Kingdom. That’s what Connor Panter , a researcher at the University of Nottingham’s School of Geography, found in a study published today in the journal Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution .
Panter analyzed how various future climate change scenarios might make different parts of the country more or less appropriate for 16 species of breeding birds of prey.

“We know that climate change is altering where wildlife is found across the world, but scientists’ understanding of how different birds of prey may respond to these changes is still relatively limited,” Panter tells Popular Science . “Raptors play important ecological roles as predators, and understanding how their distributions might change is important for informing future conservation efforts.”

Panter investigated a “middle-of-the-road” climate-change scenario and a “worst-case” climate-change scenario in the U.K. Today, there are 42,570 square miles of suitable habitat for peregrine falcons. Under the middle-of-the-road scenario, that could increase by 40.6 percent by 2060, and under the worst-case scenario, it could increase by 73.5 percent by 2080.

Hen harriers ( Circus cyaneus ), golden eagles ( Aquila chrysaetos ), little owls ( Athene noctua ), long-eared owls ( Asio otus ), western barn owls ( Tyto alba ), and western marsh harriers ( Circus aeruginosus ) could also see increases. Suitable habitats for common buzzards ( Buteo buteo ), European sparrowhawks ( Accipiter nisus ), and tawny owls ( Strix aluco ), aren’t predicted to change much in any scenario. But British short-eared owls ( Asio flammeus ), red kites ( Milvus milvus ), merlins ( Falco columbarius ), and Eurasian goshawks ( Astur gentilis ) will likely lose significant amounts of suitable land.

Ultimately, Panter’s work emphasizes that climate change will probably not impact all birds of prey in the same way, even if they live in the same areas. This could represent a significant problem for conservation, because future efforts aiming to safeguard these species will have to take these differences into consideration, according to Panter.

“It is also important to recognise that an increase in the area suitable for a species does not necessarily mean that its population will grow or that it will become more widespread,” Panter says. For example, “whether peregrine falcons can occupy newly suitable areas will depend on numerous other factors, including the availability of prey, nesting opportunities, threats from humans and interactions with other species.”

Dark energy camera captures ethereal Betta Fish Nebula
The supernova remnant's neutron star could fit inside Tuscon, Arizona.

Ghostly blue clouds about 6,800 light-years from Earth are all that remain of an ancient cosmic demise . These and other details are visible in the most recent look at a supernova remnant classified as SNR G295.5+09.7. Depending on how you see it, SNR G295.5+09.7 likely earns at least one of its nicknames: the Betta Fish or Mermaid Nebula.

A supernova remnant encompasses vast swirling waves of dust, gas, and stellar material created in the wake of a star’s death. SNR G295.5+09.7 exploded between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago in the Centaurus constellation, ejecting its outer layers of matter to collide with interstellar space’s own gases. The energy from these interactions subsequently caused the region to glow, which is now detectable by highly sensitive instruments. In this case, astronomers imaged the Betta Fish nebula using the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera (DECam) located at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile.

Although impossible to see with the naked eye, the supernova remnant contains the last vestige of its prior life in the form of a neutron star. The incredibly, miniscule dense object is what’s left from a star that was once multiple times the mass as our sun. Even now, SNR G295.5+09.7’s neutron star is larger than the solar system’s anchor—cramming about 1.4 times the sun’s into a sphere barely 12-miles in diameter. As the National Science Foundation’s National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory noted in its announcement , the stellar object is so small that it could fit inside the city of Tucson, Arizona.

However, the Betta Fish Nebula almost never happened. If the dynamics were slightly different, the massive stellar object’s collapse could have generated a black hole instead of a neutron star. If that were the case, the glowing swirls of cosmic material would likely never escape the black hole’s unfathomable gravitational pull.

The first attempt at a rescue was unsuccessful. The sea turtle was swimming in deep water with low visibility, so it could not be reached. But by the next day, the team saw the turtle swimming in an area of the river easier to access.

The roughly 70-pound turtle is now receiving behind-the-scenes care at the Aquarium of the Pacific. According to the aquarium, the fishing line caused a severe constriction injury on its the sea turtle’s left flipper. The reptile also swallowed some of the fishing line, risking damage to its internal organs.

“When the sea turtle came to us, it had a fishing line constriction that caused severe damage to its flipper,” Aquarium of the Pacific veterinarian Dr. Brittany Stevens said in an emailed statement. “Despite all efforts over the past few months, unfortunately, the left flipper could not be saved and had to be amputated to aid in the turtle’s recovery.”

This is not the aquarium’s first experience with three-flippered turtles. The team rescued and rehabilitated a green sea turtle named Porkchop, who was released into the wild in February. Porkchop has since been spotted by aquarium volunteers who monitor sea turtles.

The turtle now named Endor is receiving wound care and antibiotics as it goes through rehabilitation, with the goal of eventually returning to the wild. Endor is a sub-adult, meaning it is past the juvenile stage, and approaching sexual maturity, but not yet a full adult turtle. The sex has not been determined and Endor was previously tagged by NOAA in 2025.

As Endor is rehabilitated, it will eventually move from the behind-the-scenes sea turtle care area to a rehabilitation area open for public viewing. Meatloaf, an over 250-pound rescued green sea turtle, is currently living in that space.

The Aquarium of the Pacific has been caring for several turtle species since 2000, including green, olive ridley ( Lepidochelys olivacea), and loggerhead ( Caretta caretta ). All sea turtle species found in U.S. waters are listed as endangered or threatened and are protected by the Endangered Species Act.

NASA spacecraft created stadium-sized crater after slamming into asteroid
The ESA's first detailed images of Dimorphos are here.

After over four years of years of anticipation, the European Space Agency has obtained images detailing the aftermath of NASA’s head-on collision with the asteroid Dimorphos. The photos and scans from ESA’s Hera spacecraft highlight the results of the Double Asteroid Redirection Test ’s (DART) intentional run-in with Didymos’ 500-foot-wide moonlet Dimorphos in 2022, revealing a stadium-sized crater, cloud of boulders, and a new, erratic orbital path.

“Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same,” Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement. “Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once!”

Michel explained that while DART flattened one side of Dimorphos into a massive crater, the rest of the space rock isn’t much different. Fields of boulders largely remain where they could be seen in DART’s photos from 2022, although the event did drastically change the binary system’s surroundings.
“Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size,” added mission scientist Michael Kueppers.
Hera employed three instruments during its first observations—a thermal infrared imager to measure surface temperature, a 25-color multispectral imager, and a monochrome camera.

The car-sized probe’s work is only just getting started, too. In December, Hera will ultimately travel to barely eight miles from the asteroids, while obtaining increasingly higher-resolution photos. The spacecraft will then deploy a pair of CubeSats to get even closer to the binary system in January 2027. If all goes as planned, one of those devices will even attempt to land on the surface of Dimorphos. The combined measurements from this phase will help researchers understand the impact’s efficiency and improve future deflection strategies.
Hera’s first images were debuted at the dinosaur hall of the Berlin Natural History Museum—an intentional choice on the team’s part.

The pumpkin’s strange journey from toxic plant to a seasonal staple
Be sure to thank mastodon poop for that pumpkin pie.

From jack-o-lanterns and cute tabletop knickknacks to pumpkin pie and the ever popular pumpkin spice latte , the iconic squash fills every nook and cranny of the fall season. But the vegetable has taken a long and strange journey to become our favorite autumnal symbol.

Logan Kistler , an anthropologist at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, is interested in the origin stories of the crops that feed humanity. And squashes have a strange one. They evolved in the Americas before corn and beans, and played an important role in the start of agriculture in the two continents, he tells Popular Science .

It’s worth highlighting that pumpkins are a type of squash. Indeed, “pumpkin” is not an official botanical term, Kistler points out. Squashes, along with zucchini and some gourds, belong to the genus Cucurbita , which is within the broader family Cucurbitaceae , which includes melons, watermelons, cucumbers, and other kinds of gourds.

“Out of this genus Cucurbita at least six different independent lineages of squashes, pumpkins, gourds, and things like that evolved in several different places in the Americas, more or less simultaneously,” says Kistler. However, “the quirky thing about this genus and about a lot of members of this family is in the wild they are unpalatably nasty. They’re incredibly bitter.”

That bitterness comes from high concentrations of cucurbitacins. The compounds are the most bitter natural substances that scientists know of. Humans can’t stomach that level of bitterness, but paleontologists have discovered that mastodons (extinct elephant-like mammals) were eating them 30,000 years ago. And that means disseminating them through their feces.

Today, there is no such megafauna in North America that can withstand wild squashes—they’ve lost their evolutionary partner. Cue humans, whose landscaping-shaping settlements give Cucurbita a new ecological niche to fit into.

“You can kind of think of it as, they lose their one mutualistic partner and then they can just kind of cozy up into this new disturbed landscape that’s created by humans. But then for that relationship to make any sense, they can’t be unpalatably bitter and they can’t be toxic,” Kistler explains.

It appears that these wild squashes had to make, “that evolutionary concession to soften the rind, become less toxic, more palatable and reap the benefits of the protection and care of human cultivators.”

It seems to have worked. The genus spread far and wide, and wherever it overlaps with humans, they are making use of it. For example, the pumpkins we use to make jack-o-lanterns every Halloween originated in Mexico approximately 10,000 years ago, and there is evidence of humans domesticating them there very early on.

Ultimately, the transition from extremely bitter mastodon snack to today’s autumnal epitome probably involved both Cucurbita ’s natural evolutionary journey as well as human intervention. “I tend to think about domestication as, at least in the early phases, the plant is adapting to life alongside humans and that has benefits to humans,” says Kistler, adding that at some point people will get involved more directly.

But it doesn’t seem like many of these earliest domestication efforts were carried out with the goal of food production. In Florida, they may have been used as fishnet floats, and in the southwestern United States they were likely put to use as containers.
They were eventually carved and—as we all know—baked into pies.

Could a giant catapult launch someone to space? Short answer: Yes.
But you wouldn't want to be the projectile. The post Could a giant catapult launch someone to space? Short answer: Yes.

For as long as humans have looked at the night sky, we’ve wondered what lies beyond Earth—and dreamed up ways of getting up there. These days, powerful rockets carrying tons of fuel are the tried-and-true method of escaping the planet’s gravitational pull and reaching space.

But what if, instead of modern rockets, we went medieval? Could a trebuchet or catapult—the massive siege weapons once used to fling stones at castles—launch a person into orbit? And if so, just how big would one have to be?
The answer requires a little imagination, a lot of physics , and a space -launching siege weapon of truly ridiculous proportions.

A catapult is essentially a giant lever used to hurl projectiles. Typically, they have a large, spoon-shaped throwing arm that’s wrenched back, creating tension, and then released, flinging an object over a great distance.

A trebuchet is a kind of catapult that uses a counterweight and gravity to launch projectiles. This machine’s long arm rests on a fulcrum, with a sling or cup for the projectile at one end and a heavy counterweight at the other.
When the arm is released, gravity pulls the counterweight downward, sending the opposite end—and its payload—soaring upward and forward.
Which is more powerful: a trebuchet or catapult?

Trebuchets are typically more powerful than catapults because they can launch heavier payloads over greater distances. So for our purposes, we’ll be focusing on a space trebuchet rather than a space catapult.

Trebuchets have been hurling heavy objects through the air for centuries. The structures are believed to have originated in China as early as the fifth century BC and eventually spread across Eurasia, becoming a formidable force in medieval warfare.
They arrived in Europe during the 12th century and quickly surpassed simple catapults .

Today, trebuchets are no longer used as weapons . But they remain popular as teaching tools for demonstrating physics principles—and for the decidedly more wholesome pursuit of seeing how far we can fling pumpkins , cabbages , and other projectiles.
Could a trebuchet send someone into orbit?
So let’s crunch the numbers: Could a massive trebuchet really blast a human into orbit? Theoretically, yes. Practically, no.

For help answering this question, Popular Science turned to Frankie Zhu , an assistant professor in space robotics at the Colorado School of Mines in Golden, Colorado. Zhu gamely agreed to do some back-of-the-napkin math to put some numbers to this wildly improbable scenario.
“It just reminds me of a classic physics problem you would encounter in undergrad,” she says.

Before we can get to the heart of the calculations, Zhu says, we need to define some initial parameters. First, because the energy required to send a human into orbit depends on both mass and velocity, we need to know our imaginary astronaut’s mass. Zhu recommends 70 kilograms, or about 154 pounds.

Next, we need to define where space—and, for our purposes, orbit—begins. The conventional boundary is the Kármán line , an imaginary line 100 kilometers (about 62 miles) above sea level that is widely used to mark the edge of space. It’s the point at which Earth’s atmosphere becomes too thin for conventional aircraft to generate enough lift to stay aloft. “An orbit at 100 kilometers would be the lowest energy orbit possible,” she says.

To orbit Earth at the Kármán line—and not plummet back to the ground—a person needs to travel at approximately 7.85 kilometers per second, or 17,500 miles per hour, the same speed the International Space Station travels while orbiting Earth. “Any less and the human would fly up and then come back down in a parabolic trajectory,” she says.

If we assume that the atmosphere doesn’t produce drag on the human as they fly, then the velocity of the person leaving the trebuchet immediately after launch needs to be at least 7.97 kilometers per second, or 17,828 miles per hour. That extra bit of speed accounts for the energy needed to climb from Earth’s surface to the Kármán line.

How Humans Are Helping Golden Jackals Conquer Europe
By unintentionally protecting jackals from larger predators, people are aiding in the expansion of a remarkably adaptable canid.

The golden jackal isn’t always the color of gold; its coat ranges from creamy beige to a rusty brown with black striations. It is, however, living in a golden age—thanks in part to the ubiquity of humans.

Native to Eurasia, golden jackals in Europe have historically been confined to the southeastern tips of the continent, mainly the Balkan countries. Over the past century, though, Canis aureus has slowly started colonizing new areas of Europe, with a steep acceleration over the past two decades. Golden jackals are expanding their range, reaching as far west as Spain and as far north as the Arctic. Scientists say the expansion represents one of the most dramatic changes in the range of a species in today’s world. New research, including genetic analysis, is revealing what’s driving the jackal’s spread and the part people play in the animal’s success.

One factor that has contributed to golden jackals’ expansion is anthropogenic climate change, which has decreased snow cover and probably revealed more suitable canid habitat. The habitat fragmentation that comes with farming and urbanization is another likely influence, since golden jackals prefer a patchy environment. The species also adapts readily to human-altered landscapes and can disperse hundreds of kilometers in search of new habitat. And, not least of all, researchers suspect that humans cleared the way for them by extirpating wolves across much of Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries.
“The fact that they did not have any competitor made it easier,” says Jennifer Hatlauf, a wildlife ecologist who manages the Golden Jackal Project in Austria .

Today, researchers estimate that around 150,000 golden jackals inhabit 23 European countries, populating a range that’s 46 percent bigger than it was in 2016 . But wolf populations are growing, too; Europe hosts roughly 23,000 wolves today, compared to an estimated 12,000 as recently as 2012.

To better understand how humans, a growing wolf population, and the expanding golden jackal population interact, Hatlauf and a large team of researchers collected and analyzed data on the presence of golden jackals from all around Europe between 2001 and 2017. The information mainly came from playback surveys: Researchers played a jackal call from a speaker and listened for the response of real jackals, identifying the presence of individuals. The team then paired this data with data on wolf and human presence.

Their recently published analysis shows that the presence of wolves is the main factor limiting the expansion of jackals—a result that strengthens the hypothesis that the decline of wolves in past centuries likely opened the door to the jackal expansion. The team also found that human settlements create a shield that deters wolves and offers a refuge for jackals.

The “human shield” hypothesis isn’t new. Researchers have long known that prey or smaller predators take advantage of human presence to escape large predators. For example, some bear mothers with cubs find refuge from adult male bears by moving close to human settlements, especially during the mating season, when the males would try to kill offspring. Prey animals, such as wild turkeys, also seem to find safety near human-inhabited areas.

In places where wolves are absent, the data shows, jackals tend to stay away from humans, likely to avoid deadly encounters with our species. But where wolves are rooted in the landscape, jackals remain within humans’ proximity. “The jackal is three times smaller, so there’s simply no chance for a jackal if you have a core area of wolf populations,” says Hatlauf. That same life strategy is probably going to apply in other areas that jackals will reach in the future as they expand even farther, she adds.

“The work is excellent,” says Luigi Boitani, chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Large Carnivore Initiative for Europe, who wasn’t involved in the research. The idea that the wolf’s extirpation played a role in the jackal’s expansion and that human presence shapes the relationship between the two species has long crossed scientists’ minds, Boitani says, but no one was able to prove it with actual data until now.

Hummingbirds often use their bills for fighting, but some species’ outsized appendages are equally useful in finding food.

Despite their diminutive size and zany colors, many hummingbird species are downright ferocious when they encounter one another at a food source. That’s likely because of the demands of their lightning-fast metabolisms. In flight, a hummingbird may flap its wings 62 times per second, and some species have heart rates that top out at over 1,200 beats per minute. Hummingbirds’ small bodies have a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and they lack insulating down, so they also lose heat quickly. They must consume two to three times’ their body weight per day in high-sugar flower nectar.

Given that flowers bloom only for a short while, that makes each meal more like a high-stakes operation than a companionable feast. Even at feeders with abundant nectar supplied by humans, hummers of both sexes often joust—chasing and stabbing at each other with long, sharp bills, among other aggressive tactics and displays. The shining sunbeam ( Aglaeactis cupripennis )—on the left in this image by conservation biologist and photographer Maxime Aliaga—is no exception. Researchers tracking the species in the Andes Mountains of Peru and Ecuador found that it regularly defended flowers within its territory from hummingbirds of both its own and other species, including sword-billed hummingbirds ( Ensifera ensifera ) like the one pictured on the right.

Sword-billed hummingbirds, for their part, aren’t slouches. They wield their beaks—which are longer than their bodies—exactly as their name suggests. But the primary purpose of the species’ outsized appendage may be to get food, rather than defend it.

Scientists believe that the sword-billed hummingbird’s unique morphology evolved in tandem with long-tubed passionflowers. That subgroup within the Passiflora genus, called Tacsonia , contains more than 60 species with flower nectar tubes 6 to 14 centimeters (2 to 5 inches) long. That’s a close match with the sword-billed hummingbird’s beak, which can reach up to 11 centimeters (4 inches). The birds and flowers also overlap in range, with 37 Tacsonia species pollinated exclusively by sword-billed hummingbirds. They are the only hummingbird species with the correct proportions to deposit pollen grains on the stigmas of these dangling, downward-opening flowers, poking into them from below to drink nectar.

In intact cloud forests, this highly specialized mutualism is a boon to both plants and pollinators. But in fragmented forests, it becomes a vulnerability: Research suggests that sword-billed hummingbirds don’t frequent deforested areas. Scientists speculate that may be partly because the long-tubed passionflowers that they observed in these zones often lose their nectar to “robber” species like bees, which drill into the flowers from the side, skipping pollination and draining the hummingbirds’ food source. With the connection to the passionflowers’ primary pollinator severed, at least four species of the plant have likely gone locally extinct in landscapes fragmented by forest-clearing. Those passionflower species that have evolved shorter nectar tubes, though, are more resilient. They can rely on other hummingbirds and bats for pollination, even when the habitat becomes less suitable for sword-billed hummingbirds.
Searching for a Bird Lost to Science
A researcher grapples with the value of his efforts to document a secretive species in Papua New Guinea.

Our luck turns during a smoke break. It is hot and dry for Papua New Guinea, and we are resting on the shoulder of a gravel road, bags and cardboard biscuit boxes scattered on limestone bedrock. The boxes, in rough shape from travel, are printed with a cartoon of a man named Henry Wopa, whose bulging muscles advertise that his eponymous product is enriched with vitamins and protein. This has made the brand a staple in parts of Melanesia where deforestation has hurt food security, including here on New Britain, an island four times the size of Puerto Rico that accounts for a majority of PNG’s raw log exports . Still, the biscuits are bland and difficult to swallow without coffee, which is running out. I am hungry, but not hungry enough for more Wopa. Instead, as my colleagues squat in broken shade rolling cigarettes, I scan the canopy, ragged from decades of selective logging.

There are 10 of us in total: six Sengseng-speaking Arawe and four outsiders, including me—an evolutionary biologist from Montana—gathered to search for a poorly known bird called the New Britain bronzewing ( Henicophaps foersteri ). This large, glimmering pigeon, endemic to its namesake island, was last confirmed alive through a specimen collected by ornithologist-turned-author Jared Diamond in 1972. The bronzewing has been seen occasionally in the years since but was never again collected and has never been photographed. This is cause for some concern. As Joe Wood, an expedition member who manages international conservation programs for the Toledo Zoo & Aquarium in Ohio, put it: “It would be nice to check in on it.”

But how, exactly, do you check in on a handful of shy birds in tens of thousands of square kilometers of forest? By asking around, to start. Jason Gregg, a graduate student in my lab at Montana State University and the expedition’s leader, has spent years thinking about how to incorporate local ecological knowledge into biodiversity surveys, along with spending many hours interviewing our Arawe crew members. About half say they’re familiar with the species—known locally as kau—but communicating across gulfs of language and culture about a bird of which there are no photographs is challenging. The night before, Thomas Sunamli, who is letting us stay on his land, explained that the bronzewing is common in disturbed habitat and feeds on the red, pine-cone-like flowers of a plant called shampoo ginger ( Zingiber zerumbet ). This contradicted our own limited understanding of the bird’s diet and need for old growth.

“It’s hard to imagine what they could be getting out of [those flowers],” Wood had said, frowning as he prodded a clump of shampoo ginger at the edge of camp. Since nectar is rarely an important part of a pigeon’s diet, I was inclined to agree.

Western methods for locating the bird have so far proven ineffective. A week of constant observation, camera trapping, and attempts to attract the bird by playing the call of its closest relative through a makeshift speaker we’ve dubbed the Bronzewing Blaster 5000 have amounted to nothing. Nor is history in our favor. In the late 1950s, zoologists Thomas and Margaret Gilliard spent three months within a few dozen kilometers of our camp, collecting some 500 specimens representing 98 species for the American Museum of Natural History. Among their findings were two species new to science. Absent was a single bronzewing. To our knowledge, no ornithologists have visited here since.

The Gilliard expedition was one of the final episodes of a heyday of scientific exploration in Melanesia that had a profound influence on the fields of ecology and evolution, arguably birthing theories such as island biogeography . This era ended in 1975, when Papua New Guinea gained independence and ended colonial license to travel freely in a region that now has near-complete Indigenous land tenure. In the interim, logging corporations felled the last grand forests of Borneo and Sumatra and began working their way through New Britain. Today, cost, logistics, lack of infrastructure, and sporadic violent crime discourage many foreign biologists from studying how the logging is affecting the island’s biodiversity.
